item.title: Evening Edition, Wednesday, October 28, 2026
item.description:
The Federal Reserve held its key interest rate at 3.75% to 4% Wednesday, but two officials voted to raise it, saying inflation is still too high. The vote was 10-2: Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack wanted a quarter-point increase. The statement says the economy is "expanding at a strong pace," job gains have kept pace with the workforce, inflation "remains elevated," and "the Committee will deliver price stability." At his news conference, Chair Kevin Warsh said energy prices have moved higher again and the Fed will fit its next move to incoming data. He also said the Fed will hold fewer rate-setting meetings: in 2027 one of its eight meetings will be devoted only to long-run strategy, and in 2028 two will be, leaving six for rate decisions. Separately, the Bank of Canada raised its policy rate a quarter point to 2.50% Wednesday, its first increase since July 2023, citing higher, more persistent inflation and energy costs, and said more hikes may be needed.

Alphabet shares fell about 7% after hours as AI spending turned its free cash flow sharply negative, while Microsoft rose about 6% on faster cloud growth. Alphabet's third-quarter revenue rose 25% to $127.58 billion, its fastest growth since 2021, and Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.7 billion. But net income fell to $26.17 billion ($2.12 a share) from $34.98 billion, hurt by an $8.66 billion loss on equity holdings, and free cash flow was negative $9.07 billion; capital spending was $51.36 billion. Search revenue rose 12% to $63.35 billion, below estimates. Microsoft said revenue at its Azure cloud business grew 48% to $33.17 billion in the quarter ended September, above estimates. Reuters noted investor worry over Big Tech's debt-funded AI buildout, expected to top $700 billion this year.

A high-speed train crash in central Spain killed at least 68 people Wednesday when one train slammed into another stopped on the Madrid-Seville line. A Renfe train hit the rear of an Iryo train halted at a red signal near Urda, in Toledo province, just before 9 a.m. local time; the two trains carried about 544 people. The Castilla-La Mancha regional government said 58 people were being treated in hospitals. Transport Minister Óscar Puente said a computer communications failure had stopped traffic and that an "inexplicable" decision to let the Renfe train proceed caused the crash. Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez declared three days of mourning, and most parties paused campaigning for Spain's general election. It is Spain's deadliest rail crash since 2013 and the second high-speed collision on the line this year, after a January crash that killed 46. Toll as of Wednesday afternoon ET; it may rise.

Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers and coined the rallying cry "Sí, se puede," died Wednesday at 96. A family spokesperson told AP she died of cancer at her home in Bakersfield, Calif., surrounded by family. Huerta co-founded the farmworkers' union with César Chávez in the 1960s, helped lead the national grape boycott and negotiated its first contracts, and spent decades organizing for labor, civil and women's rights. She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2012. Earlier this year she said Chávez had sexually abused her in the 1960s. Gov. Gavin Newsom ordered flags at California's Capitol lowered in her honor.

Google's new top AI model, Gemini 4 Carbon, is going first only to vetted cyber defenders because of its skill at finding and exploiting software flaws. Google says Carbon leads benchmarks for finding vulnerabilities, validating exploits and writing patches, and ranks first on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index; those claims are Google's own. Access starts through Google's Fairwind program for security teams, and Google says it is taking part in the U.S. government's voluntary pre-release model testing. It will open to developers, businesses and consumers later, at introductory pricing of $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens. CEO Sundar Pichai said on Alphabet's earnings call Wednesday that Carbon outperforms its predecessor, Argon, "on almost every domain."

Mary Peltola's campaign aides and Senate Democrats' campaign arm helped recruit a second "Dan Sullivan" onto Alaska's ballot, the New York Times reported; both deny it. Citing interviews, text messages and documents prepared for a possible lawsuit, the Times reported that people working with Peltola's campaign and senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee took part in a broader "ballot composition project" to recruit would-be spoilers, including Daniel J. Sullivan, to draw votes from Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. Former campaign manager Elisa Rios told the Times that Peltola was not directly involved but was "definitely aware"; the Times said Rios later tried to retract her comments. Peltola's campaign said it "has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign," and the DSCC said it "is not involved with Dan J. Sullivan." The Times noted ballot-stacking is common and generally legal. After the report, President Trump demanded that Peltola and Daniel J. Sullivan be removed from the ballot. A Justice Department suit seeks to block certification of a close result; Judge Sharon Gleason has fast-tracked motions to dismiss it before the Nov. 3 election.

Congo's Ebola outbreak has passed 10,000 cases, with nearly 5,000 deaths, the World Health Organization said, making it the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded. Congo's Health Ministry counted 10,141 cases as of Monday. The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment, has spread to eight provinces; it is the largest of Congo's 17 Ebola outbreaks and second only to West Africa's 2014-2016 epidemic. More than 2,600 people have recovered, and a ring-vaccination trial of the Ervebo vaccine has begun in Bunia. Kenya's count stays at nine cases and two deaths, all linked to its first imported case; 20 contacts have been released from quarantine. The U.N. allotted more than $2 million for Kenya's response. A CDC order announced Tuesday requires air travelers entering the U.S. to attest they have not been in Congo in the past 21 days.

The taxpayer-funded TV ads promoting President Trump were blocked again Wednesday, this time by a federal judge in Washington in the Democrats' lawsuit. U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan granted the Democratic National Committee a temporary restraining order barring the administration from developing, airing or distributing the ads, paused a $20 million Office of Management and Budget allocation for them, and ordered DHS and OMB to tell the contractor, LMD Agency, to stop. The order lasts 14 days. It has little practical effect before the Nov. 3 election because a federal judge in New York had already ordered the ads halted through Nov. 8 in a separate case.

item.title: Morning Edition, Wednesday, October 28, 2026
item.description:
The Biden-era methane rules for oil and gas wells would be loosened under an EPA proposal President Trump announced Tuesday at a Texas rally. EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin and Trump unveiled the proposal in Lubbock. It would create separate, lighter standards for low-producing "marginal" wells (or, under a second option, for conventional wells), rescind the Super Emitter Program that let certified outside monitors flag large methane leaks, build a repair window into leak rules for covers and vent systems, and return to 95%-efficient flaring as the standard for gas from oil wells instead of requiring it to be piped to market. EPA says the changes would save $45 billion and add an estimated 210 million barrels of oil and 1.41 trillion cubic feet of natural gas. It is a proposal: it takes effect only after a public comment period and a final rule. The 2024 rules, known as OOOOb/c, were estimated to cost $18 billion when finalized.

Israel's vote count puts Netanyahu's bloc ahead but short of a majority, with about three-quarters of ballot boxes counted and no clear winner. Partial Central Elections Committee results with 76.8% of ballot boxes counted (as of 10:58 a.m. Israel time) give Netanyahu's bloc 54 of the Knesset's 120 seats, Gadi Eisenkot's bloc 47 and the Arab-led Joint List and Ra'am 19; 61 are needed to govern. Likud is the largest party. Seat numbers are projections from vote shares and will shift: double-envelope ballots, including soldiers', are counted later. Netanyahu's bloc ran ahead of most exit polls, which had it near 50.

The Tampa Bay Rays avoided a World Series sweep, rallying for two runs in the 12th inning to beat the Milwaukee Brewers 4-3 and force Game 5. Milwaukee led the series 3-0 and went ahead 3-2 on rookie Cooper Pratt's home run in the top of the 12th. In the bottom half, a throwing error by third baseman Joey Ortiz put the leadoff man on, Jonny DeLuca's single tied it, and pinch-hitter Ben Williamson's bases-loaded chopper won it. The Rays are the fifth team down 3-0 in a World Series to win Game 4; the previous four lost Game 5. Game 5 is Wednesday at 8 p.m. ET at Tropicana Field.

Gulf Arab countries have been told by the U.S. to prepare for a possible "short, intense" military campaign against Iran after the midterms, the Wall Street Journal reports. The Journal, citing people briefed on the conversations, said the messages went through diplomatic and military channels; it reported that a Patriot missile-defense battery is moving from Texas to the region, troops have been moved from exposed bases, and another carrier strike group and a Marine expeditionary unit are expected next month. It said Trump has not made a final decision. The White House declined to comment on "sensitive military plans that may or may not exist" and said Trump "keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon." At his Lubbock, Texas, rally Tuesday, Trump said, "You'll see Iran in a couple of weeks." Separately, IAEA chief Rafael Grossi told the UN Security Council on Oct. 27 that his agency has seen no activity to repair Iran's nuclear sites damaged in the 2025 and 2026 strikes, but that Iran still has not given inspectors access to verify its roughly 440 kilograms of highly enriched uranium.

Cassidy Hutchinson, the former White House aide who testified against Trump about Jan. 6, will not be indicted after a grand jury refused, people familiar with the case say. A federal grand jury in Washington rejected the Justice Department's request Tuesday, two people familiar with the matter told the AP. The case, handled by DOJ's Civil Rights Division, centered on her 2022 testimony to the House Jan. 6 committee, including her account that Trump lunged for the steering wheel of his vehicle, which Secret Service officials disputed. In a hearing on another matter, a division lawyer told a magistrate judge the grand jury had not agreed to a proposed indictment without naming the defendant. The refusal does not bar prosecutors from trying again. It is the latest grand jury rebuff in cases against people Trump has called political enemies.

Israel's election produced no clear winner, exit polls show, with neither Netanyahu's bloc nor his opponents near the 61 seats needed to govern. Polls closed at 10 p.m. Israel time (4 p.m. ET). Exit polls from Channels 11, 12 and 13 gave Netanyahu's bloc 50 of the Knesset's 120 seats and the Jewish-led opposition bloc 52 or 53. Netanyahu's Likud was projected as the largest party with 24 to 25 seats, ahead of Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar! at 21 to 23. Arab-led parties were projected to win a record 17 or 18 seats, up from 10. Pro-government Channel 14 and i24 News showed better numbers for Netanyahu's bloc (60 and 55). Turnout was unusually high. The Central Elections Committee is counting votes, and official results can differ from exit polls; President Isaac Herzog will decide who gets the first chance to form a government, a process that could take weeks.

A CDC order will require every air passenger flying into the U.S. to sign a statement that they have not been in Congo in the past 21 days. The order, signed Oct. 22 and published in the Federal Register on Tuesday, applies to flights departing at or after 11:59 p.m. EST on Nov. 3 and runs through Dec. 18 unless changed. It covers every flight landing in the U.S., including connections; airlines must keep each signed statement for 42 days, and knowingly false statements can be prosecuted. Medical-evacuation flights and people CDC exempts on humanitarian grounds are excluded. CDC says Congo's Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak had reached 9,455 confirmed cases and 4,561 deaths as of Oct. 18; the order adds to the entry suspension already in place. Separately, a Swiss woman with Ebola diagnosed in Nigeria was flown to Geneva University Hospitals on Monday and is stable, Geneva health officials said.

The Federal Election Commission's electronic filing system has been offline since Monday night after hacking attempts, a week before the midterms, Reuters reported. An FEC electronic filings officer wrote in an email seen by Reuters: "We have a bad actor attempting to breach FEC systems. As a result, we've had to temporarily shut down our web facing services." The FEC's status page says filing has been down since about 10 p.m. ET Monday; in a statement the agency said only that the system is offline and its IT staff are working to restore it, and declined to say what caused it. Past reports can still be searched. The outage blocks the 24- and 48-hour reports that show late spending by super PACs and other groups. The FEC does not run elections, and voting is not affected. CISA referred questions to the FEC; the FBI did not immediately comment.

A Biden-era rule letting immigration judges pause some deportation cases stays thrown out after the Supreme Court declined to restore it Tuesday. In a brief unsigned order in City of Baltimore v. Texas (No. 26A500), with no noted dissents, the court refused to pause a June consent judgment between Texas and the Justice Department that vacated the 2024 "administrative closure" rule. Chief Judge Reed O'Connor in Wichita Falls entered that judgment the same day Texas sued, at both parties' request. Baltimore, New Haven, Columbus and Centro Legal de la Raza, which called the deal collusive, were denied permission to join the case; their appeal continues at the 5th Circuit.

U.S. Ambassador Mike Waltz and Cuba's foreign minister got into a shouting match at the UN General Assembly during debate on the U.S. embargo. As Waltz accused Havana's leaders of corruption, the Cuban delegation interrupted, and Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez accused him of lying and demanded a point of order; the session was briefly suspended. The assembly votes Wednesday on its annual nonbinding resolution condemning the embargo, which passed 165-7 with 12 abstentions last year. The clash follows Secretary of State Marco Rubio's Oct. 23 public call for Cubans to work with the CIA.

Boeing shares fell nearly 10% after it said it will miss its 737 production and 500-jet delivery targets this year. CEO Kelly Ortberg said the 737 MAX will reach 47 jets a month in early 2027, not this past summer as planned, because wing production is lagging; Boeing still targets 52 a month in the second half of 2027. Third-quarter revenue rose 4% to $24.2 billion and the net loss narrowed to $116 million from $5.34 billion a year earlier; the adjusted loss of 34 cents a share was wider than the 21 cents analysts expected. Boeing projected $3 billion in free cash flow next year, below Wall Street estimates. Shares fell 9.6% to about $170 in afternoon trading, their worst day since April 2025, Reuters reported.

FBI agents searched billionaire donor Stephen Cloobeck's Beverly Hills mansion Tuesday in the federal investigation of former Rep. Eric Swalwell. The search began around 7 a.m. PT on North Roxbury Drive. The FBI confirmed an operation "related to an ongoing criminal investigation" and said court documents are sealed; AP and ABC7 reported it is tied to the Swalwell probe. Swalwell stayed at the home before he resigned from Congress in April and ended his campaign for governor amid sexual misconduct allegations, which he denies. Cloobeck, who has said he cut ties with Swalwell, was not home; his lawyers said he "continues to have faith in the judicial process." Agents seized Swalwell's devices and searched his Washington home in August.

Consumer confidence rose in October, the Conference Board said, as easing gas prices lifted Americans' mood. The index rose 7.5 points to 91.7 from a revised 84.2 in September. The Present Situation Index rose 8.6 points to 120.4 and the Expectations Index rose 6.9 points to 72.6. The survey cutoff was Oct. 21.

Florida's entire Atlantic coast, from Nassau County to the Keys, is under coastal flood warnings, with wind advisories reaching inland to Orlando through 8 p.m. Tuesday. National Weather Service offices in Jacksonville, Melbourne, Miami and Key West issued the warnings early Tuesday, citing moderate to significant flooding at high tide; coastal roads may close and low-lying homes and businesses will flood. The Jacksonville and Melbourne warnings, which include the St. Johns River basin, run until 2 a.m. Friday; Palm Beach, Broward and Miami-Dade warnings run until 8 p.m. Wednesday, with breaking waves of 8 to 13 feet off Palm Beach. Wind advisories for northeast gusts up to 40 mph cover Orange, Seminole, Osceola and the coastal counties until 8 p.m. Tuesday.

ACA marketplace enrollees would have to confirm their income, citizenship and residency every year before subsidies renew, under a CMS proposal starting with 2028 coverage. The proposed rule (CMS-9873-P), published in the Federal Register on Tuesday with 30 days for comments, carries out the Working Families Tax Cut law. Marketplaces could not automatically renew advance premium tax credits unless enrollees provide or confirm their information between Aug. 1 and Dec. 31 of the prior year; the first window would open Aug. 1, 2027. CMS's own analysis estimates 332,500 fewer people would enroll each year and about $1.9 billion a year less in premium tax credits starting in 2028.

Washington's East Potomac Golf Course can't lose more trees while a lawsuit proceeds, a federal judge ruled Monday; Trump said he will appeal. U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued a preliminary injunction that also requires 10 days' written notice before any irreversible change to the 106-year-old public course, and she declined the government's request that she step aside. She wrote that workers cut at least 400 trees over a holiday weekend after the government said it would not. Trump said late Monday he would appeal and that the course will still close Nov. 15 for 15 months of renovation.

Anthropic, the maker of the Claude AI models, filed publicly Monday to sell shares on the Nasdaq under the ticker "ANT." The S-1 filed with the SEC does not yet set a share count or price range; Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are the lead banks. The filing shows revenue of $16.29 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.16 billion a year earlier, and a net loss of $80.7 billion, most of it a $72.4 billion non-cash charge on the value of convertible notes. Anthropic filed confidentially in June; AFP reported it plans to sell shares in mid-November, and AP said the offering could top SpaceX's record $86 billion IPO in June. Separately, Meta on Monday launched a $35 billion stock sale to fund AI spending ($22.5 billion of common stock through forward sales and $12.5 billion of mandatory convertible preferred shares) and plans up to about $60 billion more later.

Brazil's main stock index plunged nearly 14% Monday, the first trading day after President Lula's reelection, while U.S. stocks rose. Trading on Brazil's B3 exchange was halted for 30 minutes at the open after the Ibovespa's drop triggered a circuit breaker, and the real fell more than 10% against the dollar, AFP reported. Lula beat Flávio Bolsonaro in Sunday's runoff. In New York, the S&P 500 rose 0.7% to 7,676.77, the Dow added 146.42 points, or 0.3%, to 52,361.58, and the Nasdaq gained 0.8%, led by AI stocks after Anthropic's IPO filing. Verizon reported 406,000 new postpaid phone subscribers in the third quarter, its best third quarter in five years, and raised its 2026 forecast.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Iranians not to pay their taxes and to stock up on fuel, predicting Iran's economy will shrink more than 25%. In an on-camera interview with Iran International on Monday, Bessent said, "My advice to the Iranian people would be: don't pay your taxes because you're not going to get anything back from the government," and said Iran has "no oil on the water" and no loadings at Kharg Island. He predicted the economy would contract more than 25% from March 2026 to March 2027 and said the next eight weeks of "Operation Economic Outcast" sanctions will be "even more intense." Treasury has not issued a readout. Separately, The New York Times reported, citing two diplomats, that Qatari mediators are working on a five-day deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for lifting the U.S. blockade; neither government has announced one.

Egypt's parliament authorized military support to help defend Saudi Arabia from Houthi attacks Monday, as talks in Tehran ended with only a pledge to keep talking. The authorization is limited to defending Saudi Arabia and applies only if Riyadh requests help, AP reported. Talks in Tehran between Iranian leaders and delegations from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey ended with an agreement to keep talking and no concrete deal announced. Yemen's Houthis said they attacked pumping stations on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline and Riyadh's airport; Saudi Arabia did not confirm the claims.

The Justice Department's emergency appeal to set aside about 20,000 California mail ballots was thrown out by a federal appeals court Monday. A 2-1 Ninth Circuit panel granted Los Angeles County's motion to dismiss for lack of jurisdiction and denied DOJ's emergency motion as moot; Judges Bennett and Sanchez concurred and Judge Bumatay dissented. The court said DOJ did not give U.S. District Judge David Carter enough time to rule on its request and called the claimed emergency "at least in part, a self-constructed one." DOJ sued Oct. 15 after sending the state a list of more than 20,000 people it called likely noncitizens. Carter holds a hearing on DOJ's request Tuesday and has said he will rule promptly.

Forty-eight noncitizens in five states face federal charges of illegal voting or falsely claiming citizenship to register, the Justice Department announced Monday. The cases are in Pennsylvania, California, Florida, New York and Nevada. Most defendants are lawful permanent residents, according to the Justice Department. They are accused of voting in the 2022 or 2024 federal elections, or in one case a June 2026 primary, and some are also charged with lying about their voting or citizenship claims on naturalization applications. The announcement comes eight days before the Nov. 3 midterms. Charges are accusations; the defendants are presumed innocent.

Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts Monday to about 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its workforce, as it pours money into AI data centers. Microsoft announced the Voluntary Exit Offer for employees at level 70 and below on participating teams in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. About 60,000 of Microsoft's 223,000 workers are eligible, the company confirmed to GeekWire. Employees decide in early December, and those who accept leave Dec. 31, CNBC reported. Some sales, marketing and engineering teams are not taking part. It follows a voluntary retirement program in April and 4,800 layoffs announced in July. Microsoft reports quarterly results Wednesday.

Maurene Comey's firing as a federal prosecutor was illegal, a federal judge ruled Monday, ordering the Justice Department to reinstate her. U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman in Manhattan found the July 2025 firing of Comey, a daughter of former FBI Director James Comey, violated the Civil Service Reform Act, the separation of powers, federal administrative law and her due-process rights. He ordered retroactive reinstatement with back pay from July 16, 2025, through Dec. 20, 2025, when she started a new job. Comey had worked on the Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell prosecutions. The Justice Department said it "disagrees with this decision and will appeal in due course." The judge has not yet ruled on her First Amendment claim and ordered further briefing.

OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra Monday, a cheaper model built for computer-use and office tasks, priced at half its predecessor's rate. The model is rolling out to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Enterprise and Edu users and to developers through the API at $1 per million input tokens and $5 per million output tokens, 50% below GPT-5.6 Terra and GPT-6.1 Sol. OpenAI said it is the first model in its line rated at the "Critical" cybersecurity threshold under its Preparedness Framework and published added safeguards.

item.title: Morning Edition, Monday, October 26, 2026
item.description:
Brazil's President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won a fourth term Sunday, beating Flávio Bolsonaro 51.8% to 48.2% in a runoff, and Bolsonaro refused to concede. With all votes counted, Brazil's electoral court said Lula led by nearly 4.4 million votes. Bolsonaro, the son of imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro, asked for the result to be annulled, objecting to Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin's decision, three minutes before polls were due to close, to keep voting open two more hours; both campaigns had requested the extension, Lula's over bus problems in São Paulo and Salvador and Bolsonaro's over heavy rain in the south. Electoral court president Kassio Nunes Marques, a Jair Bolsonaro appointee, said the extension did not affect the results. Bolsonaro led the Oct. 4 first round by more than 2.2 million votes; it is the first time since military rule ended in 1985 that the first-round runner-up won. Lula, a vocal critic of President Trump, takes office again Jan. 5, 2027.

Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey sent senior delegations to Tehran on Monday to try to head off renewed war between Iran and the U.S. and Israel. Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin were to meet Iran's top security officials and negotiators to push for a deal between Tehran and Washington, two regional officials told AP; an Iranian official confirmed their arrival. Saudi Arabia said the aim was to find ways to de-escalate tensions. Qatari mediators were in Tehran on Sunday. Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesman said the window for diplomacy had not closed, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned Sunday that Iran or its proxies could attack before Israel's election on Tuesday.

A federal appeals court panel sharply questioned the Justice Department's bid to stop California from counting about 20,000 ballots from voters it says may be noncitizens. In a rare Sunday hearing, Judge Mark Bennett, a Trump appointee, asked how the court could order relief inconsistent with California law under the Constitution's Elections Clause and said, "I don't see how we have jurisdiction," since the district court has not yet ruled. Judge Gabriel Sanchez, a Biden appointee, pressed DOJ on which third parties supplied its list; the DOJ lawyer could not say. Judge Patrick Bumatay, also a Trump appointee, focused on the harm when noncitizens vote. The panel did not rule. California says the list is inaccurate and complying before the Nov. 3 election would be disruptive; more than 3 million Californians have already voted.

Serbia's longtime leader Aleksandar Vučić conceded Sunday's parliamentary election to a student-led movement that spent two years protesting his government. Vučić said his party projects the Students' List will win 135 to 140 of Parliament's 250 seats and his Serbian Progressive Party about 105. The election commission's preliminary count, with most polling stations reporting, put the Students' List at 52.54% and Vučić's list at 39.29%, on turnout of about 69%. Vučić, who resigned the presidency last month to run for prime minister and had been endorsed by Russian President Vladimir Putin, blamed independent media and alleged foreign interference. The protests began after a train station canopy collapse in Novi Sad killed 16 people in 2024. Crowds celebrated in Belgrade and other cities.

Justice Cristiano Zanin granted a request from Lula's campaign, which said authorities in several cities were restricting voters' access to public transportation. A fire at a Pacific Seafood plant on the Newport, Oregon, bayfront forced a one-mile "go now" evacuation Sunday over possible ammonia contamination. The Lincoln County Sheriff's Office issued a Level 3 evacuation order for a one-mile radius around the plant at 203 SW Bay Blvd. after the fire broke out Sunday morning. Officials opened a shelter at Sam Case Elementary School. No injuries were reported, and the cause is under investigation.

Coastal Palm Beach, Broward and Miami-Dade counties are under a coastal flood warning from 2 a.m. Monday to 8 p.m. Tuesday as king tides reach major flood stage. The National Weather Service in Miami said moderate flooding is expected around each high tide, reaching major flood stage Monday and Tuesday. It said numerous roads may be closed and low-lying homes, businesses and some critical infrastructure will be inundated. Storm Boelo killed a man in Scotland and cut power to more than 160,000 properties across the U.K. on Sunday, with gusts above 80 mph. Police Scotland said a 60-year-old man was killed by a falling tree near Castle Douglas in Dumfries and Galloway around 10:30 a.m. The Energy Networks Association said more than 160,000 properties were without power at 3 p.m. local time. The Met Office's amber wind warnings ran into Sunday night, and rail, flight and ferry services were disrupted. It is the second named storm to hit Britain in days, after Storm Austen.

A bus carrying mourners home from a pastor's funeral collided with a truck on Kenya's Nairobi-Mombasa highway Sunday, killing 24 people. The crash happened near Mtito Andei; about 24 other people were injured, and two of the dead died later in the hospital. Kenya's National Transport and Safety Authority said preliminary reports point to a head-on collision, with improper overtaking a possible factor. It came three weeks after 17 people died in a crash on the same highway.

A shooting near Florida A&M University's football stadium during homecoming in Tallahassee injured 12 people Saturday night, six of them children. Eleven people were shot and one was hurt while fleeing, Tallahassee Police Chief Lawrence Revell said; at least three were seriously injured. Police said a fight broke out before the shots were fired just before 8 p.m. near Bragg Memorial Stadium, after FAMU's homecoming game. Revell said the victims were six adults and six juveniles, the youngest 11, and that one victim is a FAMU student. He called it an isolated incident involving two or three people. No arrests had been made, and police had no person of interest early Sunday.

The Archdiocese of New York agreed to pay $800 million to about 1,300 people who say they were sexually abused by clergy, Archbishop Ronald Hicks confirmed Saturday. Hicks confirmed the deal in an email to clergy and said it is not final until the parties sign it, which is scheduled for the week of Nov. 6. It is the second-largest settlement by a U.S. Catholic archdiocese, after Los Angeles agreed to pay $880 million in 2024, and would end more than seven years of lawsuits filed after a 2019 New York law gave survivors more time to sue. The two sides had agreed on a framework in May. Survivors' attorney Jeff Herman said each claimant can take at least $250,000 or seek more through an individual review, and that the archdiocese must publish a list of credibly accused clergy. The archdiocese covers Manhattan, the Bronx, Staten Island and seven counties north of the city, with about 2.5 million Catholics.

Ukraine's Starlink satellite links were restored Saturday after more than a week of slowdowns, and Elon Musk said SpaceX had throttled them over drone strikes. Musk wrote on X that Ukraine's military "violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week," and said the U.S. government controls Starshield, SpaceX's military version. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said speeds were back to normal Saturday morning, and Ukraine's defense minister said connections were stable. Commanders had said the slowdown cost drones and disrupted missions. President Trump said he did not make the call, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth denied any administration role.

About 410,000 people marched across France on Saturday over school funding and living costs, and the Paris march ended in clashes with police. The interior ministry counted 110,000 marchers in Paris; unions put the national total near 800,000. Police fired tear gas and water cannons in Paris and used tear gas in Lyon, Marseille, Strasbourg and other cities. The Paris prosecutor's office said 64 people were arrested in connection with the Paris march. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez had deployed up to 70,000 officers, and authorities banned rallies in Lyon, Nice and Montpellier. The Louvre, Orsay and other major museums closed for the day.

Flooding in the Four Corners region forced at least 20 more overnight rescues in New Mexico's San Juan County, with more rain forecast Saturday. Rescues ran from Farmington west to Shiprock, where power was out and the U.S. 64 bridge was closed; county officials said 200 to 300 people may have been rescued since the flooding began, and by noon Saturday they believed no one else was trapped. Evacuated areas stayed closed, Bloomfield ordered new evacuations as the river rose, and officials said river water is contaminated with raw sewage. In Colorado, La Plata County declared a local disaster and closed the Animas River to all boats. Officials said rivers could rise again with up to another inch of rain.

Iran said Saturday it is still open to reviving its interim deal with the U.S., even as its military chief vowed U.S. warships will never enter the Gulf. Iran's ambassador to Pakistan, Reza Amiri Moghadam, told AP that Tehran recently offered through Pakistan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if Washington lifts its naval blockade, and said President Trump rejected it. President Masoud Pezeshkian said on state TV that "the cowards (Americans) messed everything up" but that Iran should still try to conclude the deal, Reuters reported. Armed forces chief of staff Ali Abdollahi said U.S. military ships will not be allowed in the Persian Gulf "under any circumstances and at any time," AFP reported. Separately, Saudi air defenses intercepted a Houthi ballistic missile fired at Riyadh on Saturday, the Saudi Press Agency said.

Israel's military pressed a multi-day operation in Hebron on Saturday after two soldiers were killed at a checkpoint, displacing hundreds of Palestinians. Two Palestinian gunmen killed two soldiers and wounded three Friday near the city before they were shot dead. The military said it is searching the Al-Jaladah and Ein Deir Baha neighborhoods for militants and weapons and will carry out demolitions. Hebron's mayor said about 1,200 people have been forced from their homes; the governor put the figure at 150 families. A Palestinian prisoners' group said about 70 people were arrested, and Israel closed the entrances to most Palestinian towns in the West Bank. Israel holds its general election Tuesday.

item.title: Morning Edition, Saturday, October 24, 2026
item.description:
U.S. embassies in Jordan, Lebanon, Qatar and the UAE are cutting staff after the intelligence chief warned Iranian plots to kill Americans are in "advanced stages." In a memo sent Friday to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton wrote that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" and that "the lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against U.S. citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries." The memo, copied to CIA Director John Ratcliffe, names no targets or countries and does not say whether attacks are imminent. The four embassies, already under "restricted operations," will stay open and staff are not ordered to leave, unlike in Saudi Arabia, where nonessential personnel and families were ordered out Wednesday. U.S. officials told AP the threats from Iran and Yemen's Houthis are behind the changes and denied they are tied to any new strikes on Iran. At a Florida rally Friday, President Trump said "we may do another little Epic Fury, or they'll agree," referring to the U.S. military campaign against Iran.

A CIA contractor was arrested and charged Friday with leaking top-secret intelligence to a romantic partner who published it on her Substack newsletter. The Justice Department said the FBI arrested Ian A. Brinksman, 42, of Washington, D.C., after searching his home, and charged him by criminal complaint in the Eastern District of Virginia with unlawfully transmitting national defense information. Prosecutors say he worked for a U.S. agency from 2020 and from 2022 as a systems-integration developer for a contractor to the same agency, holding a Top Secret/SCI clearance. The FBI affidavit says articles by "Individual 1" mirrored classified reports he accessed on at least five occasions in 2026, some at the top-secret level; Reuters identified the newsletter as Capital & Empire by Aída Chávez. CIA Director John Ratcliffe said the agency referred the case. His federal public defender declined to comment. Charges are allegations; he is presumed innocent.

President Trump's tariffs on Canadian goods under a 1930 trade law will cover a revised product list from Oct. 30, under a proclamation he signed Friday. The proclamation, issued under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, drops products such as plywood sheets, some paper products, certain machinery and refrigeration equipment, and some packing crates and boxes, and adds certain valves, carpets, waste products and others, the White House said. The tariffs, first announced July 20 and modified Sept. 8, apply whether or not goods qualify under the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement and come on top of Section 232 duties. The White House cited Canada's retaliatory tariffs on about $20 billion of U.S. exports. The tariffs face a challenge at the Court of International Trade.

Up to 400,000 barrels of emergency oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve will go to Phillips 66's Lake Charles, La., refinery, the Energy Department said Friday. The department said the exchange from the reserve's West Hackberry site, for immediate delivery, offsets temporary disruptions to crude deliveries to the refinery and supports fuel supplies for Louisiana and nearby markets; Phillips 66 must return the oil plus extra premium barrels. The refinery can process about 264,000 barrels a day. Reuters noted the reserve is already at its lowest level since 1982. A Phillips 66 spokesperson said the company does not anticipate impacts to Lake Charles operations.

Immigrants held by ICE in Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi have no constitutional right to a bond hearing, the full federal appeals court there ruled Friday. The 5th Circuit, sitting as a full 17-judge court, ruled 10-7 that people who entered the U.S. without being admitted and are held under 8 U.S.C. 1225(b)(2)(A) are not entitled by the Fifth Amendment's due process clause to hearings on whether they are dangerous or likely to flee, however long their deportation cases take. It reversed lower-court orders that had freed three men, two from Mexico and one from Honduras, who had lived in the U.S. 14 to 22 years and were turned over to ICE after traffic stops, and it overturned a July panel ruling that had required bond hearings within 90 days. Judge Cory Wilson wrote for the majority that detainees can end their detention "at any moment by agreeing to leave the country." Judge Leslie Southwick, writing for six dissenters, said the court had built "an impenetrable wall between the Constitution" and long-term residents; Judge Dana Douglas wrote that unchecked power to detain indefinitely "echoes fearfully from history." Texas and Louisiana hold the largest numbers of immigration detainees in the country. The ruling deepens a split with other appeals courts, and the Supreme Court agreed this month to decide the related question of whether immigration law itself requires bond hearings. DHS general counsel James Percival called it a "big win." The National Immigration Project, which represents the men, said it opens the door to more people being locked up and is weighing whether to appeal.

Brent crude closed at $116.72 a barrel Friday, its highest since April, and the Dow fell 653 points as oil weighed on stocks. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 652.82 points, or 1.2%, to 52,215.16; the S&P 500 lost 39.75 points, or 0.5%, to 7,623.68, its second straight weekly loss; and the Nasdaq slipped 53.52 points, or 0.2%, to 25,955.34, a day after its biggest drop since June, Reuters and AP reported. Nearly three of every four S&P 500 stocks fell. Brent rose 3.1% and U.S. crude 3.8% to $103.27, driven by Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and a tanker oil spill off the UAE, Reuters reported. Separately, the Energy Department authorized an emergency loan of up to 400,000 barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to Phillips 66's Lake Charles, La., refinery after a crude-delivery disruption.

Alaska's Senate result could not be certified if Sen. Dan Sullivan loses narrowly, under a Justice Department lawsuit Trump said Friday he ordered. The suit, United States v. Alaska, filed Thursday in federal court in Alaska against the state Division of Elections, argues that a second candidate on the ballot, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., will confuse voters. It asks the court to bar certifying the result if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses and would have won had the other Sullivan's votes gone to him, pending an investigation, citing the National Voter Registration Act. "I'm the one that said do it," Trump told reporters Friday as he landed for a rally in Florida. The Alaska Supreme Court earlier kept Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot; he will appear without a party label, while the senator is listed as the Republican incumbent. Democrat Mary Peltola called the suit "the corruption AK is fed up with." The election is Nov. 3, 11 days after the filing.

Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, Jordan, on Friday, killing at least seven people and wounding 40. State television footage showed at least three gunmen approaching the church and firing; a mourner said the shooting began 15 minutes into the service. The government called it an attack "by unknown assailants" and said investigations are under way; it did not say whether anyone was caught. Two of the wounded are in critical condition, the health minister said. King Abdullah II vowed "the harshest penalties," Prime Minister Jafar Hassan blamed "terrorist ideology and blind extremism," and Jordan declared three days of national mourning. Karak, about 110 miles south of Amman, has a Christian minority. Arab News reported Saturday that the death toll had risen to eight. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the attack.

Russia and Ukraine agreed to a local ceasefire in occupied Oleshky so aid can enter and civilians can leave, in a deal Melania Trump brokered. The White House said the truce in the Kherson-region town starts Oct. 29 and lets non-military teams from both countries visit residents and arrange evacuation to Russia or Ukraine. Ukraine's chief negotiator, ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, confirmed the deal and told AP the ceasefire will start Tuesday, cover the Kherson region and nearby areas needed for the operation, and last several days. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed it, said all civilians who want to leave may do so and that the evacuation will take at least several days, and praised the first lady's role. It is not a wider ceasefire.

Nikki Cole Floris, 46, who led the FBI's now-dissolved Foreign Influence Task Force as a deputy assistant director from 2019 to 2022, and Bradley Benavides, 56, its section chief through the 2020 election, are each charged by criminal complaint with one count of false statements to Congress. Prosecutors say both told the House Judiciary Committee in 2023 that the task force had no role in the Hunter Biden investigations, and that Benavides said he learned of the FBI's possession of the laptop from Wikipedia; the U.S. Attorney's Office for D.C. says documents and witnesses contradict that testimony. Charges in a complaint are allegations, and both are presumed innocent.

item.title: Morning Edition, Friday, October 23, 2026
item.description:
New Hampshire can bar student IDs even as backup proof of identity at the polls on Nov. 3, the Supreme Court ruled Thursday, pausing a judge's order. The Court granted Secretary of State David Scanlan's emergency application (Scanlan v. Coalition for Open Democracy, No. 26A512) and paused a federal judge's Oct. 2 and Oct. 5 orders while the case is appealed to the 1st Circuit and, if sought, the Supreme Court. A state law passed this year removed student IDs from the list of accepted photo IDs for getting a ballot; Scanlan's guidance then barred them for any purpose, including under a backup provision that lets officials weigh other evidence of identity. U.S. District Judge Joseph Laplante left the law in place but blocked that guidance. The unsigned order, quoting a 2020 precedent, said lower federal courts "should ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an election." Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented, writing that the judge's order left the state's rule untouched and only corrected a publicized misstatement of what the law requires. The Republican National Committee backed the state. New Hampshire has a closely contested U.S. Senate race this year.

Apple's first foldable iPhone, the $1,999 iPhone Duo, goes on sale Friday in the U.S. and more than 70 other countries. Announced Sept. 9, the iPhone Duo has a 7.6-inch inner screen that folds to a 5.4-inch outer screen, the A20 Pro chip and a titanium body, and starts at $1,999 in the U.S. Preorders opened Oct. 16, and it reaches 28 more countries Oct. 30, Apple said.

Brent crude rose above $114 a barrel Friday, its highest since early May, after Saudi Aramco evacuated its headquarters amid Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. Brent futures were up 79 cents at $113.96 a barrel by 4:10 a.m. ET, after touching $114.72, the highest since May 4, and are on track for a third straight weekly gain of almost 4%, Reuters reported; U.S. crude was up $1.10 at $100.57. Saudi Aramco on Thursday ordered staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran, on the Gulf near Bahrain, as fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis intensified, Reuters reported. Saudi Arabia's state news agency said air defenses intercepted and destroyed drones and missiles aimed at Riyadh and the kingdom's south early Friday.

Up to $150 million in Defense Production Act money will go to restart a U.S. refinery and expand fuel refining, President Trump announced Thursday. Presidential Determination No. 2026-11, issued under Section 303 of the Defense Production Act, declares domestic petroleum production, refining and logistics capacity essential to national defense. The Energy Department said the Title III money will expand petroleum production, storage and logistics at refineries across the country to raise output of gasoline, diesel and jet fuel, and that project selection is ongoing. Trump announced the plan at a rally in Sioux City, Iowa.

Quest Diagnostics, the national lab company, says hackers got into a test-ordering system and likely accessed some patient records. In a regulatory filing Thursday, Quest said it learned on Oct. 21 of unauthorized access to its Quanum Lab Services Manager, a system some clients use to place test orders and receive or look up results. The company said it believes "certain patient records" were accessed, but how many patients and which records were affected is still unknown and under investigation. Quest said it notified federal law enforcement, hired outside cybersecurity experts, and that the incident has not materially disrupted its operations. Quest said the breach was not related to the widely reported PHP security flaw.

Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas, the chamber's top Democrat, was indicted on federal charges of leading an illegal marijuana business with family members. The eight-count indictment unsealed Thursday in the Eastern District of Virginia charges Lucas, 82, and six others, including her two daughters and her grandson, with a racketeering conspiracy involving marijuana distribution, money laundering, honest-services fraud through bribery, maintaining drug-involved premises, possessing firearms in furtherance of drug trafficking, and wire fraud. Prosecutors allege the group acquired and sold 100 kilograms or more of marijuana and that Lucas used her post as chair of the Senate Finance and Appropriations Committee to shield the business and influence legislation; FBI Director Kash Patel put the five-year scheme at an estimated $4.5 million. Lucas, a senator since 1992 and president pro tempore since 2020, surrendered Thursday morning and was due in federal court in Norfolk. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the investigation had run for several years and rejected claims it was political. In a social media post, Lucas did not address the charges but said, "I will not be intimidated," according to Reuters. Virginia's state senators are not on the ballot this year.

The Nasdaq fell 2.6% Thursday and the S&P 500 lost 1.2%, its worst day since July, as AI stocks tumbled and oil rose. The S&P 500 fell 93.74 points to 7,663.43 and the Nasdaq composite dropped 694 points to 26,008.86, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average edged up 11.89 points to 52,867.98, AP reported; most U.S. stocks actually rose. AI stocks swung lower on worries about high interest rates and heavy spending, after Meta projected billions more in future costs. Brent crude rose 3.7% to $112.80 a barrel, its highest in about five months, after Iran said seven tankers were hit near the Strait of Hormuz and after the attack on a Saudi airport. Treasury yields fell sharply as investors moved into bonds.

Mississippi's ban on DEI programs in public schools and colleges can be enforced after a federal appeals court threw out a judge's order that cited made-up material. Treasury's proposed rules for the law barring large investors from buying single-family homes were released Thursday; the ban starts Jan. 7, 2027. Virginia state Sen. L. Louise Lucas, the chamber's top Democrat, was indicted on federal charges of leading an illegal marijuana business with family members. The Commerce Department signed letters of intent for up to $389 million in CHIPS research awards to four companies making power chips. Fusion company Helion would get up to $175 million and Commonwealth Fusion Systems up to $85 million for high-voltage and fusion-related power semiconductors, Vertical Semiconductor $73 million and Sibelco $56 million. item.title: Morning Edition, Thursday, October 22, 2026
item.description:
Saudi Arabia's King Fahd International Airport in Dammam was attacked late Wednesday, killing two people and injuring eight, Saudi aviation authorities said. Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said Thursday the dead were a Saudi citizen and an Indian national living in the kingdom; the toll was first reported as one. The eight injured, from Saudi Arabia, India, Yemen, Bangladesh and Nepal, had injuries ranging from minor to severe. Flights were diverted during the attack; the authority said Thursday that operations had resumed and air traffic was back to normal, and that damage was being assessed. Saudi authorities did not say who was responsible, and the Iran-backed Houthi rebels issued no statement; the airport, near Bahrain and Qatar, has been hit before in a wave of Houthi strikes on Saudi airports. Separately on Wednesday, Saudi Arabia's Energy Ministry said debris from an intercepted drone aimed at a processing facility at Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oil field killed a Filipino and a Nepali worker and injured two others; it said oil operations were not affected. The attacks came the same day the State Department ordered non-emergency U.S. diplomats and their families to leave Saudi Arabia.

Seven oil tankers caught fire or were damaged overnight in and near the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's state TV said, citing its Revolutionary Guard navy. Quoting the Guard navy, Iranian state television said four tankers were hit while transferring oil between ships and caught fire, and three were damaged and stopped after hitting naval mines. It gave no casualty figures or flags. The claims have not been independently confirmed: the British military's UK Maritime Trade Operations center had not reported the attacks, though AP notes some shippers have been reluctant to report incidents. If verified, it would be the most vessels damaged in the waterway in one day since the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran began Feb. 28. The Guard again threatened U.S. bases in the region if the U.S. keeps helping guide commercial ships through the strait. Brent crude rose 3.2% to $112.27 a barrel and U.S. crude 2.8% to $99.80 early Thursday; S&P 500 futures were down 1%.

Homeland Security's door-to-door questioning of possible noncitizen voters was blocked in nine states Wednesday night by a federal judge, through Election Day. U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín in San Francisco issued a preliminary injunction barring DHS "elections-related field operations and field interviews" likely to involve people officials know or should suspect are U.S. citizens, in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin, until polls close Nov. 3. She found the practice of armed agents questioning residents at their homes about immigration status and voting likely violates the Voting Rights Act's ban on intimidating people who help others vote, and cited a "high likelihood of error" in the lists used to pick targets. She wrote that investigating unlawful voting is not itself unlawful. The order is paused until 5 p.m. Friday so the government can appeal. Plaintiffs include San Francisco, Santa Clara, the California Nurses Association, National Nurses United and the Voto Latino Foundation. DHS did not immediately comment; Justice Department lawyers had argued that blocking such investigations would harm the public interest.

Kyiv was hit by Russian ballistic missiles and drones overnight, killing one person and wounding 22, hours after the Kremlin agreed to resume peace talks. Ukraine's State Emergency Service said the strikes damaged homes, transportation infrastructure and other civilian sites in several districts; in the Dniprovskyi district on the Dnipro's east bank, one person was killed and six wounded, including a child. On Wednesday, Kremlin adviser Yuri Ushakov said Vladimir Putin agreed "in principle" to restart three-way talks with the U.S. and Ukraine after Nov. 10. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy backed the talks but said, "We'll see what happens this time."

President Trump said the U.S. is not negotiating with Iran and that "something one way or the other" will happen "fairly soon," speaking late Wednesday. Asked on the tarmac after his South Carolina rally whether he was negotiating with the Iranians, Trump said: "No, I think we're not negotiating with. We are going to have something one way or the other that'll happen fairly soon. Most people seem to think it's after the election, and we're going to see what happens." He also said U.S. strikes had "taken out" Iran's military, navy and air force. On Ukraine, he said the push for talks is "the closest I've seen to maybe working out." Iran's foreign minister said Wednesday that Tehran remains open to diplomacy but is ready to defend itself.

PHP, the programming language behind most websites, released emergency fixes Wednesday for two critical flaws that can let attackers take over web servers remotely. The flaws, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (nicknamed "php2shell"), are memory-handling bugs that PHP says can allow remote code execution without logging in; PHP rates both 9.2 out of 10 in severity. PHP says every installation serving web requests is at risk, with the danger highest on Apache servers running mod_php, where a demonstrated exploit works before any website code runs. Fixed versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 came out about 9:40 a.m. ET; PHP 8.1 and older get no official update. PHP runs on about 69% of websites whose server language is known, according to tracker W3Techs, including WordPress, Drupal and Magento sites. CISA issued an alert saying it had not seen exploitation as of publication, while security firms watchTowr and Cloudflare reported attack attempts. Governments in the Netherlands, Finland and France took some websites offline as a precaution, Reuters reported, and the FBI warned that the flaws put sensitive data and networks at risk, AP reported. Researchers at Calif, OpenAI and Wiz found the flaws using AI tools and reported them to PHP starting Aug. 11.

Non-emergency U.S. diplomats and their families must leave Saudi Arabia, the State Department ordered Wednesday, citing escalating Houthi attacks. State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said the order covers "non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only," citing Iran-backed Houthi attacks on Saudi civilian airports and other critical infrastructure that have caused civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions. The U.S. Embassy in Riyadh issued a security alert the same day warning of possible further Houthi attacks after recent deadly strikes, including on Riyadh's airport. U.S. officials told Reuters that other U.S. missions in the Gulf will also order family members to leave; the department did not address other missions. Washington had returned some diplomats to the region in recent months after pulling many out when the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran began in late February. The Saudi travel advisory remains Level 3, "Reconsider Travel."

Meta must pay New Mexico $25 billion for deceiving Facebook users about privacy, a state judge ruled Wednesday, the biggest fine ever against the company. State District Judge Francis J. Mathew wrote that Facebook's deception was intentional: "Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false." A jury in September found Meta liable for more than 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer-protection law over statements tied to the Cambridge Analytica scandal, in which a personality quiz harvested data from about 87 million profiles. The state had sought $35 billion to $40 billion; Meta argued for $3.4 billion at most. The penalty dwarfs the $5 billion FTC fine of 2019, and under the state constitution the money goes to education. Meta said it is "confident we will prevail on appeal" and that the ruling makes it "all but impossible to do business" in New Mexico; interest accrues during the appeal. New Mexico was the only state to take these claims to trial.

SNAP food-aid fraud was the target of a nationwide Justice Department crackdown that charged or convicted more than 40 people, officials said Wednesday. The Justice Department's Fraud Division, the Agriculture Department and USDA's inspector general said the first National USDA Benefits and Program Fraud Enforcement Surge, run Sept. 1 through Oct. 21 with 13 U.S. attorney's offices and the Utah attorney general, involved schemes with nearly $45 million in intended losses, nearly $42 million of it against SNAP. The largest case is an Ohio indictment accusing two Chicago store operators of running about $29.7 million in fake transactions with stolen EBT card data. Other cases include stolen benefits used to buy infant formula for resale and stores trading cash for benefits. Attorney General Todd Blanche and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins announced the results; DOJ said charges are allegations and defendants are presumed innocent.

Ukraine peace talks among Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. will resume after Nov. 10, the Kremlin said Wednesday, as Russia freed jailed American Stephen Hubbard. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Russia agreed in principle to the three-way talks, focused on post-war security arrangements, after President Vladimir Putin met U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg; it was Witkoff's ninth in-person meeting with Putin and came a day after he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Oslo. No ceasefire or deal was announced. As the talks began, Putin told Witkoff that Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired teacher detained in April 2022 and sentenced to six years and 10 months on mercenary charges he denies, was at the airport waiting to fly home with him. President Trump said he had asked Putin to free Hubbard and that it was not a prisoner swap.

Stablecoin issuers overseen by the OCC now have final federal rules under the GENIUS Act, which the bank regulator issued Wednesday. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's final rule sets requirements for reserve backing, redemption, risk management, custody, licensing, capital and operations for payment-stablecoin issuers under its jurisdiction. It takes effect Jan. 18, 2027; OCC-supervised issuers generally need approval before issuing payment stablecoins in the United States. The OCC said it will announce later when it begins accepting applications and waiver requests, and issuers with substantially complete pending applications may seek waivers.

The Bureau of Prisons' new limits on transgender inmates' care stay blocked after the Supreme Court refused Wednesday to let the policy take effect. In a one-sentence unsigned order in Trump v. Kingdom (No. 26A416), the court denied the administration's application to pause a lower-court injunction; Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito would have granted it. The February 2026 policy would end hormone therapy and "social accommodations" such as wigs and makeup for transgender federal inmates. Senior U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth blocked it on Aug. 26, and a divided D.C. Circuit panel refused to pause his order. The class-action case continues in the lower courts.

Subtropical Storm Josephine formed off the U.S. East Coast Wednesday with 65 mph winds and is forecast to move northeast, away from the United States. At 5 p.m. AST the National Hurricane Center put the storm, formerly the system it tracked as AL93, near 37.4 N, 69.5 W, moving north at 6 mph with a minimum pressure of 990 mb. Before it was named, the NHC said high winds, coastal flooding and dangerous surf were expected along parts of the East Coast for the next few days regardless of development; the slow-moving offshore low has driven coastal flooding and high surf from the Outer Banks to the Jersey Shore this week.

Meta's third-quarter revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion, and Tesla's beat estimates at $28.05 billion, the companies reported after the bell Wednesday. Meta earned $9.86 billion, or $3.83 a share, after a $9.89 billion charge for its settlement with 52 state attorneys general over teen mental health; without it, earnings would have been $7.40 a share. Meta forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $73 billion to $76 billion, said capital spending was $34.91 billion in the quarter, and said headcount fell 15% from a year earlier to 66,775; it also announced a new Class C common stock. Tesla's revenue compared with $28.10 billion a year earlier; net income fell 29% to $787 million, automotive revenue fell 3% to $20.56 billion, and free cash flow was $1.53 billion as capital spending came in at $4.73 billion, below analysts' forecasts.

The Nasdaq rose 1.1% Wednesday as a strong SpaceX profit report lifted tech stocks; the S&P 500 gained 0.6% and the Dow 0.7%. The S&P 500 closed at 7,757.17, up 44.60 points; the Dow rose 360.21 points to 52,856.09; and the Nasdaq composite gained 278.04 points to 26,702.86. SpaceX shares rose about 8% after it reported third-quarter revenue up 161%, and Super Micro Computer raised its outlook on demand for AI systems.

item.title: Morning Edition, Wednesday, October 21, 2026
item.description:
California state workers are on a one-day strike Wednesday, the first in the history of SEIU Local 1000, the largest state-employee union. The union represents more than 100,000 state employees, including auditors, nurses and counselors, and is picketing in cities across the state. Members voted to authorize the strike earlier this month, saying the state has not bargained in good faith since their contract expired in June. The union wants raises of 20% over three years, a larger state contribution to health-care costs and more flexibility for remote work; Gov. Gavin Newsom ordered state workers back to the office four days a week by July 1 and last month vetoed a union-backed bill on office mandates. The California Department of Human Resources said departments have contingency plans and it remains available at the bargaining table.

X account DataRepublican alleges leaked recordings show progressive groups planned to declare the federal government illegitimate if certain "red lines" are crossed. Unverified. UNVERIFIED ALLEGATION. The claims below are DataRepublican's and have not been independently verified; High Impact News Daily has not reviewed the recordings. In posts since Oct. 18 it calls "The Democracy Files," the account says it obtained "thousands of new transcripts and hundreds of recordings" from private calls, which it says come from the Renew to Thrive group and associates. It alleges Renew to Thrive sits inside a little-known "United Democracy Alliance" that it describes as a "control plane" of leaders from groups such as 50501 and Indivisible, and says National Security Leaders for America, led by retired Rear Adm. Michael E. Smith, is credited with "operationalizing" it. It says the audio outlines "a sequence of 'redlines'" under which the federal government "should be declared illegitimate," with an Insurrection Act invocation against protesters "one of the most discussed," and an earlier post says planned responses include "handing that legitimacy to Democratic governors." It says the audio shows the idea was "shopped" to governors, while adding that governors "do not have to explicitly sign on." The account calls this a "coup"; that is its characterization. A third post Tuesday night alleges the groups took advice from foreign officials with experience in political transitions abroad, though it says that video "doesn't prove" the meeting caused later events. No charges, investigations or official statements about the claims have been announced, and no public response from the named groups or people could be found as of early Wednesday. The account released a book the same week and urges readers to vote Republican.

Florida executed William Reaves, 77, on Tuesday, its 18th execution this year, for the 1986 killing of a sheriff's deputy. Reaves was pronounced dead at 6:12 p.m. after a three-drug injection at Florida State Prison near Starke. He was convicted of first-degree murder in the shooting death of Indian River County Deputy Richard Raczkoski. He was the eighth Florida prisoner over age 70 executed this year. Florida set a state record of 19 executions last year and would tie it if an execution scheduled for next month is carried out.

Boeing's 737 Max 10, the largest 737, was cleared by the FAA on Tuesday to carry passengers after years of delays. The FAA issued an amended type certificate and an updated production authorization, so the jet can now be delivered to U.S. and foreign airlines; Boeing says deliveries begin in the coming months. The FAA required changes under the 2020 Aircraft Certification, Safety, and Accountability Act and NTSB recommendations, including an enhanced angle-of-attack sensor system that Boeing says will become standard across the Max family. Boeing says the certification program included nearly 1,000 test flights, and that more than 30 customers have ordered 1,555 Max 10s, over 30% of the Max order book. The plane was introduced in 2017 and originally planned for delivery in 2020. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy handed over the documents at Boeing's Everett, Wash., plant.

Iran will not hold talks with Washington until its demands are met, its leaders told Pakistan's army chief, a key mediator, in Tehran on Tuesday. President Masoud Pezeshkian met Field Marshal Asim Munir to discuss mediation, according to Iranian media. Parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf said the U.S. could not regain Iran's trust until it meets the seven conditions Iran set last month for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, including ending the U.S. blockade of Iran's ports, lifting sanctions on its oil exports and ending hostilities on all regional fronts. Security chief Mohsen Rezaei delivered the same message and said all enriched nuclear material will stay in Iran. Pakistan's earlier mediation helped produce an interim deal in June that unraveled when fighting resumed weeks later. Vice President JD Vance said earlier this month that Iran must make a "meaningful" cut in its enrichment capacity to end the eight-month war.

A challenge to ICE arrests at churches and synagogues was revived Tuesday when a federal appeals court ruled 27 religious groups can seek to block the policy. A split D.C. Circuit panel (2-1) reversed U.S. District Judge Dabney Friedrich, who had ruled the Christian and Jewish groups lacked standing for a preliminary injunction, and sent the case back for her to reconsider their request. The groups challenge the Jan. 20, 2025, Homeland Security memo that rescinded the decades-old "sensitive locations" policy limiting immigration enforcement at places of worship. Judge Florence Pan, joined by Judge Robert Wilkins, wrote that the government "announced a plan to ramp up enforcement" and the groups showed a credible threat. Judge Neomi Rao dissented, calling the claimed harms speculative. The ruling does not itself block the policy.

The death toll from Monday's drone strike on a market in Abyei, on the Sudan-South Sudan border, has risen to at least 153, AP reported Tuesday. The strike hit Amiet Market and a nearby fuel depot, setting off a large fire; the morning edition reported at least 73 dead. Reuters also cited an official saying more than 150 people were killed. Local officials blamed Sudan's military; that has not been independently confirmed. Abyei is claimed by both Sudan and South Sudan.

The Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program, a new $25 million Justice Department fund, will pay tipsters $10,000 to $30,000 when their tips lead to fraud charges. The Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division runs the program, and the Treasury Department is committing $25 million to it. Awards are paid at the department's discretion once criminal charges are filed, rather than after a case ends, and tipsters can still qualify for larger awards under other programs. It covers federal health care fraud, with priority on hospice, home health care, day care and special services, and fraud on programs run by the Agriculture Department (such as SNAP), Labor, HHS, HUD, Education, Veterans Affairs, the Department of War and the Small Business Administration. People who took part in the fraud are not eligible. Tips can be submitted now at america.gov/fraud. President Trump announced the program with Vice President JD Vance, who chairs the White House fraud task force.
