Online dating services must warn users who got messages from members banned for fraud, under one of 10 bills President Trump signed into law Tuesday. The Romance Scam Prevention Act requires the fraud-ban notices. The other laws make Arizona's Chiricahua National Monument a national park; give ministers and certain religious workers two years to ask the IRS to revoke their exemption from Social Security coverage (the Clergy Act); order Labor Department training to spot human trafficking; order a Commerce study on making in the U.S. high-demand products now imported because of supply limits; extend Interior's authority to collect oil and gas permit fees; and transfer or place in trust land in Arizona, Washington, Alaska and Mississippi.

British fighter jets will fly defensive missions over Saudi Arabia to help shoot down Houthi missiles and drones, Britain's Defence Ministry said Tuesday. RAF Typhoon jets will protect Saudi cities and critical infrastructure and will not strike the Houthis, the ministry said. Britain will also send an A400M transport plane and military advisers and extend its air-to-air refueling support for Saudi air operations, including those against Houthi military targets in Yemen. Defence Secretary Wes Streeting cited the Houthis' targeting of King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Britain already has air-defense equipment and personnel in the kingdom.

U.S. housing starts fell 5.2% in September, and contracts to buy existing homes dropped to the lowest level on record, two reports showed Tuesday. Builders started homes at a 1.221 million annual rate, down from 1.288 million in August and 7.4% below a year earlier, the Census Bureau and HUD said; single-family starts fell 4.6% to 859,000, and building permits slipped 0.2% to 1.40 million. Separately, the National Association of Realtors' pending home sales index fell 7.3% to 66.0, the lowest since the series began in 2001, and was down 11.3% from a year earlier, with declines in all four regions. NAR chief economist Lawrence Yun blamed fast-rising mortgage rates.

Netflix shares fell about 5% after hours Tuesday after its fourth-quarter revenue forecast came in below analysts' estimates. Netflix reported third-quarter revenue of $12.87 billion, up about 12% and in line with its own forecast, and earnings of 87 cents a share. It forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $13.44 billion, below the roughly $13.51 billion analysts expected.

SpaceX's revenue rose 161% to $14.6 billion in the third quarter and it earned $4.4 billion, the company reported Tuesday. A year earlier SpaceX lost $1.1 billion. Its artificial-intelligence segment brought in $7.6 billion, up from $813 million, helped by cloud-services deals and its August purchase of Cursor; Starlink and other connectivity revenue rose 69% to $5.2 billion, with 13.6 million Starlink consumer subscribers. Capital spending reached $48.1 billion in the first nine months. It was SpaceX's second quarterly report since its June listing on Nasdaq.

item.title: Morning Edition, Tuesday, October 20, 2026
item.description:
Russian missile and drone attacks killed at least four people and wounded 27 in the Kyiv region overnight into Tuesday, regional police said. Kyiv regional police said three people were killed and six wounded at a production and storage building in Obukhiv district, and a woman was killed and 21 people wounded, eight of them children, in Bucha district, where 199 houses and 25 apartment buildings were damaged; Vyshhorod district was also hit. Separately, a drone struck morning commuter traffic near the Kyiv-Odesa highway at the edge of the capital. Officials gave differing early counts for that strike: the Kyiv regional prosecutor's office said three were killed and four hurt in Chabany, and Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said at least one was killed and six hurt on the city side; those figures are not included in the police total. Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 165 drones overnight and 115 were shot down or suppressed. Russia also hit energy sites in the Odesa region. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was in Oslo seeking more support from Norway and Finland, and said he spoke with Secretary of State Marco Rubio about Patriot interceptors, intelligence sharing and Starlink.

Alberta voters rejected starting a path toward leaving Canada in Monday's referendum, with about 77% choosing to remain, early unofficial results showed. With more than 1 million votes counted, 77% backed "Alberta should remain a province in Canada" and 23% backed starting the constitutional process toward a binding separation referendum, according to Elections Alberta's unofficial results. The vote was not itself an independence vote. Official results are due Oct. 29. Prime Minister Mark Carney said "Albertans chose Canada." Premier Danielle Smith, who called the vote but opposes independence, is to address the province Tuesday evening. Late poll openings kept more than 100 polling stations open longer. The ballot carried nine other questions.

The Tampa Bay Rays won the American League pennant Monday, beating the Cleveland Guardians 7-3 in Game 6, and will face Milwaukee in the World Series. Tampa Bay took the AL Championship Series 4-2 after trailing 1-0 and 2-1, winning the last three games. Yandy Díaz and Junior Caminero each hit two-run homers. Freddy Peralta, named ALCS MVP, allowed one run in 5 1/3 innings. It is the Rays' third pennant and their first World Series trip since 2020. Neither team has won a World Series, so either will be a first-time champion, the first such World Series since 1980. Game 1 is Friday night in Milwaukee.

U.S. farmers will get $8 billion in one-time payments to offset higher diesel and other harvest costs, under a USDA program announced Monday. The Harvest Fuel Relief program is paid from Commodity Credit Corporation funds and run by the Farm Service Agency. Payments use a uniform formula based on planted acres, USDA cost-of-production estimates and projected yields and prices, not farmers' actual fuel bills. Payment rates for major commodity crops are due in November, with the method for other commodities later. Crop insurance is not required. Applications are not open yet. It follows the $12 billion Farmer Bridge Assistance program.

North Carolina's stricter absentee-ballot envelope rules stay in place for the midterms after a federal judge refused Monday to block them. U.S. District Judge Thomas D. Schroeder denied a preliminary injunction in North Carolina Alliance for Retired Americans v. North Carolina State Board of Elections. Voting groups and two voters challenged State Board guidance under which a ballot not sealed inside the inner container-return envelope, or found outside it, is spoiled and must be replaced even if the outer envelope is sealed (2024 guidance had accepted a ballot if either envelope was sealed), and a signature-verification step. The judge cited the Supreme Court's Purcell principle against changing election rules once voting is underway: about 123,828 absentee ballots had been requested as of Oct. 8, the State Board said 31,582 had been cast by the Oct. 14 hearing, in-person early voting began Oct. 15, and Election Day is Nov. 3. Voters whose ballots are spoiled can get a new ballot or vote in person. The North Carolina Republican Party and the RNC joined as defendants. The ruling is preliminary, not a final decision on the merits.

The 9/11 plea deals for Khalid Sheikh Mohammed and two co-defendants stay void after the Supreme Court refused Monday to hear their appeals. The unsigned order denied review in Mohammad v. United States and bin 'Atash v. United States, leaving in place a D.C. Circuit ruling that then-Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin lawfully withdrew the 2024 agreements, which would have traded guilty pleas for life sentences instead of possible death sentences. Justice Brett Kavanaugh did not take part in Mohammed's case. A military judge has set the trial of Mohammed, Mustafa al Hawsawi and Walid bin 'Atash for June 2028. On the same order list, the court also turned away former NLRB member Gwynne Wilcox's challenge to her firing by President Trump, and agreed to hear cases on race in Montgomery County, Md., magnet-school admissions and on the federal ban on home distilling.

A drone strike on a market in Abyei, the disputed Sudan-South Sudan border area, killed at least 73 people Monday, the region's information minister said. Abyei's caretaker information minister, Yohana Akol Ngor, told Reuters about 73 people were killed and 19 wounded. He blamed Sudan's army but gave no evidence. South Sudan's foreign ministry said drones hit a market north of Abyei town; it gave no casualty count and summoned Sudan's ambassador in protest. Doctors Without Borders (MSF) said it was treating more than 20 wounded, including critical and burn cases, at Ameth Bek Hospital. Abyei, an oil-rich area, is claimed by both countries. Sudan's war between its army and the Rapid Support Forces began in April 2023.

Storm Adam's floods have killed at least four people in eastern Spain, where officials kept residents of 145 towns indoors for much of Monday. Valencia regional president Juanfran Pérez Llorca confirmed three deaths in his region: a 79-year-old woman who drowned and a man who had a heart attack, both in Oliva on Monday, and a woman who died at sea in Sagunto on Sunday. A woman swept away by floodwater in Cabrera de Mar, near Barcelona, also died. More than 450 people were rescued and about 800,000 people were under the stay-home order in southern Valencia and northern Alicante, since lifted; some areas got up to 700 liters of rain per square meter. Andalusia's emergency service reported a fifth death Monday, a driver killed when a boulder hit his car in Benaoján, Málaga.

A Russian drone struck a crowded park in Nova Vodolaha, in Ukraine's Kharkiv region, Monday afternoon, killing six people, including a 1-year-old girl. The strike hit the town's central park about 4:30 p.m. local time, Kharkiv regional prosecutors said; regional head Oleh Syniehubov said 15 people were wounded, seven of them children. Among the dead were a girl just over a year old, killed in her stroller, her mother, who died in the hospital, and an 11-year-old girl. Prosecutors opened a war-crimes investigation and said the drone appeared to be a jet-powered Geran-3.

DeepSeek AI products must be removed from federal civilian agencies' computer systems and purchases, under a Homeland Security Department order filed Monday. The order, "Exclusion and Removal of DeepSeek Products from Federal Civilian Executive Branch Information Technology Systems and Procurements," went on public inspection at the Federal Register on Oct. 19 and is set for formal publication Oct. 20. DeepSeek is a Chinese artificial-intelligence company.

The Nasdaq rose 1.1% Monday as AI and chip stocks recovered some of last week's losses; the S&P 500 gained 0.4% and the Dow slipped 0.1%. Canada's inflation rate rose to 3.1% in September from 3.0% in August, driven by gasoline prices, Statistics Canada said Monday. Gasoline prices were up 27.8% from a year earlier and fuel oil 57.8%, as crude rose amid the Middle East wars. Excluding gasoline, prices rose 2.2%. item.title: Morning Edition, Monday, October 19, 2026
item.description:
Duties on most reviewed Canadian softwood lumber fall to about 25% from about 35% starting today, under final Commerce Department reviews. Commerce's annual antidumping and anti-subsidy reviews, covering 2024 shipments and published in the Federal Register Monday, Oct. 19, set new cash-deposit rates for lumber entered on or after today. For about 220 other reviewed companies, the combined rate falls to 24.75% from 35.16% (antidumping 10.64%, down from 20.53%; anti-subsidy 14.11%, down from 14.63%). Company rates: Canfor's antidumping rate falls to 17.00% from 35.47% and West Fraser's to 4.71% from 9.65%; Resolute's are 13.13% antidumping and 12.42% anti-subsidy, and West Fraser's anti-subsidy rate is 15.31%. Exporters never reviewed keep the original 6.04% antidumping and 14.19% anti-subsidy rates.

Indonesia's main stock index fell to a six-year low Monday, after index provider MSCI said it may drop the country from its emerging-market indexes. The Jakarta Composite fell more than 5% early Monday, Oct. 19, after an 11.6% plunge Friday, and closed down about 3.6%. MSCI said Friday it is considering moving Indonesia from "emerging market" straight to "standalone" status over opaque ownership and trading; a final decision is expected by June. The Indonesia Stock Exchange cut its daily down limit for stocks to 7% from 15%. The rupiah weakened to 18,040 per dollar, near June's record low of 18,190. Goldman Sachs estimates a full removal could trigger about $5.6 billion in passive fund outflows. Foreign investors have net sold $4.88 billion of Indonesian stocks this year, Reuters reported.

Russia hit Kyiv with ballistic missiles and drones overnight into Monday, killing one person and injuring eight, local authorities said. The attack damaged buildings and infrastructure in three Kyiv districts, including a medical facility in a 25-story residential building in Solomianskyi, where a fire broke out, a private medical facility and a metro station in Desnianskyi, and schools and a sports facility in Dniprovskyi. Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and 269 drones across the country; air defenses destroyed or suppressed 243 drones and four missiles, and strikes were recorded at 25 locations. Russia's Defense Ministry called it a "massive strike" and said it hit a data center, a drone and missile logistics hub, a drone-parts plant and a locomotive depot, and struck a bulk carrier at sea about 80 miles southwest of Odesa; those are Russian claims.

Australian lawmaker Helen Haines was critically injured when an SUV hit her outside her office Monday; police arrested the driver and found a knife. Haines, 65, an independent first elected to Parliament in 2019, was struck by a Toyota Land Cruiser outside her electoral office in Wangaratta, Victoria, police said; her family confirmed her identity. A passerby detained the 43-year-old driver at the scene. Police seized a knife from inside the vehicle and said they are investigating whether it was intentional. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said police recorded more than 1,000 threats against politicians in the 2025-26 financial year.

Israeli police arrested 10 people Monday over weekend settler attacks on a Washington Post photographer and European diplomats in the occupied West Bank. Police did not identify the suspects or their roles. On Friday, a crowd of young male settlers beat Post photographer Heidi Levine in the village of Abu Falah, breaking several ribs and vertebrae. On Saturday, masked settlers attacked Belgium's consul general, French and Polish diplomats and Catholic representatives visiting Taybeh. Police said the Shin Bet security agency, the border police and the military took part in the investigation, and that Monday's operation also targeted closed-military-zone violations and illegal construction. U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee called the attack on Levine a "despicable act of terror."

French President Emmanuel Macron condemned rioting and looting in a televised address Sunday, as arrests from France's cost-of-living protests passed 2,400. Macron voiced the public's "anger" and "shame" and blamed much of the violence on "insurrectionist elements from radical far-left groups, joined by numerous criminals." He said looters will have to pay for the damage, and he told prefects to work with mayors to protect public buildings and businesses in the coming weeks, including by banning protests when necessary. Authorities put Saturday's turnout at about 550,000 (organizers said 800,000). Paris police reported 855 arrests in the capital region, with 557 people still in custody. Fire gutted Limoges' 19th-century City Hall. Paris police said one person died of a heart attack, and a 17-year-old girl in Mulhouse lost an eye. Saturday's first count was at least 272 arrests.

Four Canadian service members were killed and dozens seriously wounded in Saturday's fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday. Carney called the fast-moving fire one of the worst tragedies for Canada's Armed Forces on Canadian soil in peacetime and said next of kin have been notified. Those affected came from bases across the country, including reservists and soldiers of Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry. He ordered flags on federal buildings lowered to half-mast. The fire began in a training area at about 4 p.m. local time Saturday; its cause is under investigation.

Albania's student-led protests reached a sixth day Sunday as Tirana police fired rubber bullets and tear gas and Prime Minister Edi Rama refused to resign. Hundreds of protesters gathered outside the Education Ministry chanting "Rama, resign." The Health Ministry said 65 people were hurt in Saturday's clashes, 37 of them police officers, and 272 have been injured since Tuesday, including 169 officers. On Saturday a fire set by protesters spread into the Supreme Court building. Protesters want better education and jobs and an end to corruption; the unrest grew out of protests against a luxury resort project linked to Jared Kushner. Rama blamed a "foreign hand" and asked whether Albanians wanted unrest or European Union membership.

U.S. warnings of Russian ballistic missile launches are reaching Ukraine again after a pause, President Zelenskyy told NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday, thanking the U.S. for restoring them. "It was blocked for some period of time. And then it was deblocked by American side. We are very thankful for this. Now it works," Zelenskyy said, adding that Ukraine got no U.S. warning during three days of ballistic attacks. He said Ukraine's generals and government believe a slowdown of SpaceX's Starlink service was "the message from American government to limit this speed, and technically SpaceX did it," and that speeds are still limited. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, on the same program, said President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio "have categorically said that no one in the Trump administration did that" and called Zelenskyy's charge "very reckless."

An airstrike on a house in Yemen's Saada province killed at least nine people, including five children, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said Sunday. The strike hit a home in Sahar district and wounded 19, the ministry said; the Houthis blamed Saudi-led coalition aircraft, and the coalition had not commented. Separately, the coalition said a Saudi National Guard AH-6i reconnaissance helicopter crashed in Saudi Arabia's Najran region near the Yemen border because of a technical malfunction, killing its two officers.

The outbreak began with a Kenyan who had lived in Congo, traveled through Uganda, arrived in Nairobi on Oct. 3 and died on Oct. 5; four more cases, including three health workers who treated him, were confirmed Saturday. By Saturday authorities had quarantined 128 of 130 identified contacts for 21 days of monitoring. The Bundibugyo strain has no licensed vaccine or specific treatment.

East Potomac Golf Links, a public course in Washington, will close Nov. 15 for a 15-month redesign, President Trump announced Sunday despite a pending lawsuit. Trump said the rebuilt course will stay open to the public and be able to host events such as the U.S. Open, PGA Championship and Ryder Cup. Park Service crews cut down 430 trees there on Oct. 10 while a lawsuit was pending, and U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes has barred further tree cutting through Oct. 26. Democracy Forward, which represents the challengers, said Sunday it will keep fighting to protect the park.

item.title: Morning Edition, Sunday, October 18, 2026
item.description:
A Ukrainian drone attack on oil facilities, logistics and data centers in St. Petersburg and the surrounding Leningrad region killed one person and injured 15, local authorities said Sunday. St. Petersburg Gov. Alexander Beglov said fires broke out at the city's oil terminal, an oil depot and industrial warehouses. Online retailer Ozon said its St. Petersburg logistics hub was on fire, and internet company VK said one of its Leningrad region data centers was attacked by drones but services were running normally. Russia's Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions overnight.

The Tampa Bay Rays beat the Cleveland Guardians 7-3 Saturday to even the American League Championship Series at two games apiece. Junior Caminero's tiebreaking double off Daniel Espino in the sixth inning put Tampa Bay ahead in Game 4 at Cleveland's Progressive Field, the Rays scored three in the seventh after a Chase DeLauter error in right field, and Yandy Díaz added a two-run homer. Rays starter Nick Martinez retired 11 straight batters after Cleveland scored first. Game 5 is Sunday in Cleveland, with Parker Messick facing Drew Rasmussen, and the series is guaranteed to return to Tropicana Field for Game 6 on Monday night. The winner faces the Milwaukee Brewers in the World Series.

The Golden State Valkyries beat the Atlanta Dream 68-64 Saturday in San Francisco to take Game 1 of the WNBA Finals. Gabby Williams scored 26 points, 16 of them in the second quarter, and made two free throws with 1:18 left to put Golden State ahead and two more with 4.1 seconds to go. No other Valkyrie reached double figures. Allisha Gray scored 19 for Atlanta in her return from a finger injury, and Angel Reese had 14 points and 12 rebounds. Game 2 of the best-of-seven series is Monday night at Chase Center; neither franchise has won a WNBA title.

A fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta killed and injured people Saturday, Canada's military said; it has not released numbers. The fire started in a training area at about 4 p.m. local time and was whipped by strong winds beyond the base, about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton. The Canadian Armed Forces said it will not confirm casualty numbers until next of kin are notified and that the full extent remains under assessment. Defence Minister David McGuinty said he could not recall an incident like it in recent memory and that RCMP were involved, calling it "soon to be an active and delicate investigation."

A drone strike on a cattle market in Nyala, in Sudan's South Darfur, killed 30 people and wounded 47 on Friday, a hospital source told AFP. The medical source at Nyala Hospital did not say who carried out the strike. The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces blamed the army, saying it used a Turkish-made drone, and said 17 women and five children were among the dead. A military source told AFP the army had stepped up strikes on RSF positions inside Nyala and that all its attacks were aimed at military targets. Nyala, Sudan's second-largest city, is the seat of the RSF's self-declared administration. The strike happened Friday, Oct. 16; this is a catch-up item.

A truck driven through a youth soccer game in Wichita, Kansas, on Saturday killed a 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man and sent 11 people to hospitals. Wichita Police Capt. Aaron Moses said the 34-year-old woman driving is in custody. He did not say whether police believe the crash was intentional: "We are still working to determine how this happened and why this happened." The injured range in age from 5 to 68, and two children were also in the truck. Authorities said there is no further threat to the public.

France's nationwide protests over rising living costs turned violent Saturday, with cars burned and shops looted in Paris and at least 272 people arrested. Tens of thousands marched in cities across France, joining weeks of high-school student protests. In Paris, police used tear gas and water cannons on masked protesters around Place de la République. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez's office reported a growing number of violent incidents nationwide, including assaults on officers, looting and damage to public buildings; protesters broke into town halls in Marseille and Lille, and the tourist office in Lyon was set on fire. The arrest count is the government's tally as of Saturday afternoon and may rise.

No Kings rallies against President Trump were held Saturday in cities across the U.S., this time urging people to vote early in the Nov. 3 midterms. The anti-Trump No Kings network, which has held marches and demonstrations for nearly two years, billed Saturday's hundreds of planned events as nonpartisan. At the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, a band played for what appeared to be a few hundred people holding signs such as "VOTE EARLY" and "HANDS OFF MY VOTE!" In Atlanta, City Councilman Michael Julian Bond urged the crowd to get others to vote before the Nov. 3 general election.

Pakistani and Afghan Taliban forces exchanged fire for hours Saturday along the border in Pakistan's Kurram district, Pakistani security officials said. Pakistani security officials and state media said troops backed by artillery destroyed Taliban posts. The officials also said troops killed an unspecified number of Pakistani Taliban militants trying to cross from eastern Afghanistan. Afghanistan's Taliban government had no immediate comment. The two countries have had repeated border clashes this year, and Pakistan has carried out airstrikes in Afghanistan. Pakistan says Pakistani Taliban leaders shelter in Afghanistan, which Kabul denies.

A second oil tanker hit a mine in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed Saturday; no one has independently confirmed it. Iran's official IRNA news agency said both tankers, each carrying about 2 million barrels of crude, caught fire after striking naval mines and the second was left immobilized, and that they had switched off tracking and used a route Iran had not authorized. The Guards did not name either ship. This updates this morning's report of the first claimed mine strike.

Pope Leo XIV left Rome's Gemelli Hospital and returned to the Vatican on Saturday, four days after surgery that removed part of his right lung for cancer. His doctors, Dr. Luigi Carbone and Prof. Stefano Margaritora, said blood tests and a chest X-ray Saturday morning showed he was fit to be discharged. The Holy See Press Office said he will lead the Angelus prayer from the Apostolic Palace on Sunday. Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni said recovery is expected to take about a week; his schedule is cleared until at least Oct. 20, and the Vatican has not announced further treatment. His next major trip, to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, is set for early November.

item.title: Morning Edition, Saturday, October 17, 2026
item.description:
The new Russia sanctions law's tariffs and most of its sanctions were waived by President Trump on Friday, days before 100% duties on big Russian-oil buyers were due. A Friday executive order implementing the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which Trump signed Sept. 18, waives the law's 500% duty on Russian goods, its 100% duties on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas making purchases on or after Oct. 18, and its duties on the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions, along with most of its sanctions sections. Trump sent Congress a certification that the waiver is in the national interest; it lasts until the President or the Secretary of State decides further action is appropriate. Russia sanctions under earlier executive orders stay in place, and the U.S. Trade Representative will keep monitoring buyers of Russian energy.

Russia attacked Ukraine overnight with more than 330 drones and missiles, killing one person and injuring at least 24, Ukrainian officials said. Ukraine's Air Force said Russia fired 332 attack drones plus ballistic and cruise missiles, and that 293 were shot down or disabled while 22 sites were hit. One person was killed and 19 injured in the Kherson region and five were hurt in Zaporizhzhia. Russia's Defense Ministry said it struck steel plants, a transformer factory and power sites in Kryvyi Rih, Zaporizhzhia and Zhytomyr. Separate Russian strikes on Friday killed at least eight people and briefly cut power to more than 1 million.

An oil tanker carrying about 2 million barrels of crude hit a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire, Iran's Revolutionary Guards said, according to Iranian state media. State media said the tanker had switched off its positioning and radar systems and tried to use a route through the strait that Iran had not authorized. The Guards later said a second tanker, also carrying about 2 million barrels, hit a mine and was left immobilized. There was no independent confirmation of either report. Maritime officials said Wednesday that a container ship and a dry bulk carrier sank near the strait after being hit by projectiles.

Brent crude oil hit $110 a barrel Friday for the first time since May as Iran stepped up attacks on shipping near the Strait of Hormuz, and stocks fell. U.S. crude (WTI) crossed $100 for the first time since Sept. 21. Iran has said it is increasing strikes in response to the U.S. blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions imposed last month. On Wall Street the Nasdaq fell 2.1%, the S&P 500 1% and the Dow 0.4%, led by AI-linked tech stocks; for the week the Nasdaq fell 4.5%, its worst week since late June, and the S&P 500 fell about 2%. Separately, Rep. Gregory Meeks introduced a bipartisan House bill Friday to block the administration's deal to let Russia release diesel to world markets.

Aden International Airport in Yemen was hit by two Houthi missiles Friday night, landing about 500 meters from a Yemenia jet preparing to leave for Cairo. Yemen's information minister, Moammar al-Eryani, said the missiles landed about 100 meters from the middle of the runway; everyone aboard flight IY612 was safe and no casualties were reported. It was the second attack on the airport in under 10 days and came a day after a Houthi strike on the presidential palace complex in Aden.

Letters with suspicious powder mailed to election offices and senators nationwide are under FBI investigation, three weeks before Election Day. The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service said they are investigating a series of suspicious mailings to secretary of state and election offices, some containing an unknown substance, and are working to identify who sent them; Capitol Police are also involved. Mailings led to election-office evacuations this week in Louisiana and Oklahoma, and offices from Minnesota to Idaho to Florida reported letters received or intercepted. Letters to the offices of Sens. Amy Klobuchar, Lisa Blunt Rochester, Alex Padilla and Kirsten Gillibrand were intercepted. Wisconsin said tests found the powder it received was not hazardous. No injuries have been reported.

A ballistic missile fired toward Yanbu, Saudi Arabia's Red Sea oil export hub, was shot down Friday, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said. Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki Al-Malki said two cruise missiles were also destroyed over the Red Sea and three drones over southern Saudi Arabia and the Riyadh region; no damage was reported. The coalition said it is striking Houthi positions in Taiz and Marib. The UN Security Council on Thursday condemned escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, including on airports and energy sites.

U.S. industrial production rose 0.7% in September, the Federal Reserve said, after a 0.1% gain in August. Manufacturing output rose 0.3%, mining 0.2% and utilities 3.5%, while motor vehicle and parts output fell 3.0%. Industrial output grew at a 2.8% annual rate in the third quarter and was 2.2% above a year earlier. Capacity use rose to 76.9%, 2.5 points below its 1972–2025 average.

Maldives police said two Maldivian Flydubai co-pilots held in the UAE in connection with the FZ1073 investigation were sent home Friday and are being questioned. Maldives Police Service spokesperson Ahmed Shiyam said the two pilots arrived in the Maldives on Friday morning and officers met them at Velana International Airport to question them and clarify information about the Sept. 30 incident. He said they have not been arrested and that police will announce any decision to take action against them. Neither the UAE nor the Maldives has said what role, if any, the two had. The UAE attorney general has said the Omani co-pilot confessed and claimed he acted alone, while investigators keep checking for accomplices or other links. No charges have been announced in the case.

Sixteen people found floating in the Pacific off Mexico's Baja California were rescued early Friday by the U.S. Coast Guard, which is searching for others. The Coast Guard answered a distress report around 1 a.m. local time and found people in the water about 140 miles west of Ensenada, with no boat in sight; one survivor said as many as 27 people had been aboard. The area is used by smugglers moving migrants to the U.S. by sea. Survivors were taken to San Diego hospitals, including one with a suspected shark bite. Mexican authorities are leading the search with Coast Guard help.

Katie Zacharia is out as White House press secretary after five days on the job, the White House said Friday. The White House said she is transitioning out of the role and that her next position will be announced later. Her short tenure followed a widely criticized first briefing. President Trump said Friday he was in no rush to name a replacement, and no successor has been named.

item.title: Morning Edition, Friday, October 16, 2026
item.description:
Tesla unveiled its long-delayed next-generation Roadster Thursday night at a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, nearly nine years after first showing it. The reveal was livestreamed starting at 8:55 p.m. ET, two weeks after an Oct. 1 date was scrapped over weather. Tesla's Roadster page now lists three versions: a two-seat road car sold by reservation, a limited-release track version with rear SpaceX cold-gas thrusters that Tesla says reaches 0-60 mph in under 1 second, and an invite-only one-seat version Tesla says "can fly." Tesla says the thruster versions are not approved for public road use. Reuters reported that the $200,000 price from 2017 has not been updated and that reservations are still $50,000; Tesla originally promised deliveries in 2020. Musk has called the car a "small potato situation" for Tesla's finances.

A 16-year-old shooter killed three children and a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday, police said; the shooter is dead. The shooting happened about 1 p.m. PT (4 p.m. ET) Thursday. Bend police said they got a call at 12:59 p.m. PT about a person shooting into a car outside Silver Rail Elementary, followed about a minute later by multiple 911 calls reporting that the person had entered the school and opened fire. Officers arrived at 1:02 p.m. and the shooter was down seconds later, police said. Police said the attacker forced his way in by shooting at locked doors and was shot by a person at the scene who pursued him into the school; he was found dead inside minutes after the first report. Police Chief Mike Krantz said the children killed were ages 5, 8 and 11. A 7-year-old child and a teacher were taken to the hospital in critical condition. The shooter's identity has not been released. Bend-La Pine Schools canceled classes and athletic events districtwide for Friday.

Pope Leo XIV has lung cancer, the Vatican confirmed Tuesday, Oct. 13, after surgeons at Rome's Gemelli Hospital removed the lower lobe of his right lung. The Holy See Press Office said tissue examined during Tuesday's operation confirmed lung adenocarcinoma, as suspected from earlier tests. Surgeons led by Prof. Stefano Margaritora removed the lobe using a video-assisted technique; the operation lasted about 90 minutes with no complications. His schedule is cleared until at least Oct. 20. In a Thursday, Oct. 15 update, his doctors said routine checks were normal, a chest X-ray showed good recovery of the operated lung, he was carrying out daily activities independently, and his recovery is proceeding as expected. The Vatican said he resumed work from the hospital and met with a senior aide. Further tests on the removed tissue are pending.

The Milwaukee Brewers swept the two-time defending champion Los Angeles Dodgers to reach the World Series for the first time since 1982. Milwaukee won Game 4 of the National League Championship Series 6-4 Thursday night at Dodger Stadium after falling behind 4-0 on a Shohei Ohtani three-run homer. Garrett Mitchell's sixth-inning home run put the Brewers ahead and David Hamilton added a ninth-inning homer. It is the franchise's second World Series trip. Milwaukee will host Game 1 next Friday against the winner of the AL Championship Series between Cleveland and Tampa Bay.

The Justice Department's lawsuit against New York City's sanctuary laws was thrown out by a federal judge in Brooklyn on Thursday, leaving the city's limits on helping ICE in place. U.S. District Judge Ramón E. Reyes Jr. granted the city's motion to dismiss the suit the administration filed in July 2025. He found the federal government lacked standing to challenge the city's ban on police holding immigrants at federal request because state law already bars that practice, and ruled that federal law does not require local governments to share release dates or other custody information. He rejected the argument that federal law overrides the city's rules, finding the federal government cannot force local governments to assist with immigration enforcement. Mayor Zohran Mamdani called the ruling a victory for New Yorkers.

The Dow closed up about 1.1%, more than 500 points, Thursday as investors moved money out of tech stocks and into Treasury bonds. The S&P 500 rose 0.3% and the Nasdaq 0.1% after recovering from an intraday drop of more than 1%; the S&P tech sector fell 0.5%. The 10-year Treasury yield fell to about 5.09%, its biggest one-day drop since Aug. 1, the Wall Street Journal reported. Nike, Home Depot and Sherwin-Williams led the Dow. The moves followed the hotter-than-expected wholesale price report and Wednesday's worst day since July for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq.

Yemen's presidential palace in Aden, seat of the internationally recognized government, was hit by Houthi missiles, killing at least two people. Officials first said two security personnel were killed when ballistic missiles struck al-Maashiq Palace; Yemen's health minister later put the toll at five dead and 16 injured. The information minister told the BBC the prime minister and other ministers were not hurt. Houthi spokesman Yahya Sarea said the group struck what it called the Saudi military's operations headquarters in Aden. Saudi Arabia's deputy foreign minister accused Iran of encouraging the Houthi escalation.

Nicolás Maduro, Venezuela's ousted leader, had a not-guilty plea entered for him in New York federal court on new torture-conspiracy charges. Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, were arraigned on a superseding indictment filed last week charging them with conspiracy to commit torture. Maduro called the charges false before Judge Alvin Hellerstein cut him off and entered the plea; Flores pleaded not guilty. Prosecutors say the couple ran a violent system of repression under which thousands of Venezuelans, including U.S. citizens, were killed, harassed or tortured. The new count adds to earlier narco-terrorism, cocaine-trafficking and weapons charges. The couple were captured in a U.S. military raid in January; trial is set for June 2027.

The International Energy Agency's members agreed to speed up release of their remaining 100 million barrels of emergency oil, including over 20 million barrels of diesel. The IEA Governing Board said about 330 million barrels have been released so far under the March 2026 collective action responding to the Strait of Hormuz crisis. Members agreed to accelerate the remaining roughly 100 million barrels, with more than 20 million barrels of diesel to go out as soon as possible, bringing total releases above the original 400 million barrels. The board cited continued tight oil markets, especially for diesel, and urged producers to raise output.

Iraq's International Development Bank and two Iranian offshore banks were sanctioned by Treasury for allegedly giving Iran access to U.S. dollars. The designations, under Operation Economic Outcast and Executive Order 13902, also cover Iranian offshore banks Jazireh International Bank and Chabahar International Bank Overseas, Dubai-based oil intermediary Sayyed Ruhollah Razavi and two of his companies, Hong Kong's Elitesphere Trading, and four Iranian exchange houses and their owners. The State Department separately designated Cuba's Banco Internacional de Comercio for serving Iran's Karafarin Bank. Their U.S. assets are blocked, and foreign banks dealing with them risk secondary sanctions. Treasury's FinCEN also issued an alert asking banks to flag possible Iranian abuse of religious charities.

Two chemical tankers off Romania's Black Sea coast were hit by drones, Romania's president said, and seven of one ship's 12 crew were still missing as of Friday. The San Marino-flagged Wine Trader was struck early Thursday about a mile outside Romanian territorial waters. Five of its 12 crew were rescued, but strong winds and rough seas hampered the search for the rest, which resumed Friday with a Black Hawk helicopter placing four rescuers aboard. The Comoros-flagged Yara J was hit inside Romanian waters late Wednesday; its crew were unharmed and it was towed to Constanta. President Nicușor Dan said both ships were struck by drones, and a NATO military source said the drones came from Russia. Both were anchored near the Sulina canal, which links the Danube to the Black Sea and is a key export route for Ukraine.

Ohio's EdChoice private-school voucher program is unconstitutional, a state appeals court ruled, though vouchers continue while the state appeals. A three-judge panel of the Tenth District Court of Appeals ruled 3-0 in Columbus City School District v. State of Ohio, upholding a Franklin County trial court that found EdChoice funds a separate school system in conflict with the Ohio Constitution. The court kept enforcement on hold pending an expected appeal. About 180,000 students use EdChoice, which became universal in 2023. Attorney General Andy Wilson said the state will appeal to the Ohio Supreme Court and that there is no immediate impact on families.

Wholesale prices jumped 1.3% in September, the biggest monthly rise since March 2022, while retail sales rose 0.8% on pricier gas. The Bureau of Labor Statistics said its final-demand Producer Price Index rose 1.3% in September after 0.5% in August, and is up 6.3% over 12 months, the most since December 2022. Goods prices rose 2.6%, the largest increase since the series began in 2009; energy rose 10.8% and gasoline 20.3%. Services rose 0.8%. Separately, the Census Bureau's advance estimate put September retail sales at $745.0 billion, up 0.8% from August and 6.3% from a year earlier; August was revised up to 1.3%. Gas station sales rose 6.4% for the month, and sales excluding gas stations rose just 0.2%.

item.title: Morning Edition, Thursday, October 15, 2026
item.description:
A school roof collapse in Peshawar, Pakistan, killed at least 28 children and a teacher and injured more than 50, AP reported. The roof fell at the private Al-Khair school in northwestern Pakistan on Thursday. A Lady Reading Hospital spokesman said all the children killed or hurt were 13 or younger. Rescuers were still searching the rubble, and the toll could rise.

Ukraine resumed drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, setting Rosneft's Ryazan refinery on fire in its first energy strike since President Trump's announced truce. Ryazan Gov. Pavel Malkov said a large drone attack caused a fire at the refinery, which handles almost 5% of Russia's refining and supplies fuel to Moscow. President Zelenskyy told the Financial Times that Ukraine paused energy strikes for three days at U.S. request but would resume because Russia kept hitting Ukraine's power grid. Russia's defense ministry said debris from downed drones caused the fire.

Russia fired 580 drones and two missiles at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine's Air Force said, killing three people in the Kirovohrad region. The Air Force said 536 drones were shot down or jammed as of 8 a.m. local time Thursday, with hits at 31 locations and falling debris at 11 more; the two Kh-59 missiles were fired from the Black Sea. The figures were preliminary and the attack was still under way when they were released. AP reported the three deaths in Kirovohrad, the hardest-hit region.

TSMC, the world's largest contract chipmaker, said third-quarter profit jumped 69% to a record T$763.1 billion (about $23.6 billion) on AI chip demand. The result for July through September beat the T$746.3 billion LSEG SmartEstimate, Reuters reported. TSMC makes chips for Nvidia and Apple, and its results are closely watched as a read on spending for AI hardware.

The FCC does not have to rule within 48 hours on Democratic candidates' challenge to cheaper campaign ad rates for party committees, the Supreme Court said. In an unsigned opinion Oct. 14 in FCC v. Brown (26A476), the Court stayed an Oct. 7 Fourth Circuit order that gave the FCC until Oct. 9 to decide the candidates' application, saying the Communications Act sets no deadline and the appeals court could not force the agency to cut short its process. The FCC's March notice saying parties engaged in coordinated activity get the law's lowest ad rates stays in place; the Court had already put the Fourth Circuit's earlier ruling on hold Sept. 4. Justices Sotomayor and Jackson would have denied the stay.

California's law requiring plainclothes federal agents to show identification cannot be enforced against them, a federal appeals court ruled. A Ninth Circuit panel (Judges Nguyen, Bennett and Collins) on Oct. 14 reversed a district judge and ordered a preliminary injunction barring California, Gov. Gavin Newsom and Attorney General Rob Bonta from enforcing Section 10 of the No Vigilantes Act against federal agencies and officers. That section requires non-uniformed federal officers working in California to visibly display ID, with criminal penalties for violators. The court said the Justice Department is likely to win its claim that the state cannot directly regulate how federal officers do their jobs under the Constitution's Supremacy Clause.

Saudi Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran was hit in a Houthi strike that damaged the offices of the oil giant's chief executive and other top officials. Two regional officials told AP the strike targeted the top three floors of a building used by senior executives, with no casualties. New explosions were also heard in Riyadh on Wednesday, again blamed on Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis. Separately, Iran's Revolutionary Guard navy said a cargo ship carrying 2,500 containers sank after hitting a mine in the Strait of Hormuz; AP could not verify it.

The State Department must open the 2027 diversity visa lottery, which it had skipped this year, a federal judge ordered. U.S. District Judge Jinsook Ohta in San Diego granted a preliminary injunction Oct. 14 in Red Eagle Law v. Rubio. She ordered Secretary of State Marco Rubio to publicly announce the DV-2027 registration period, including dates, the entry website and requirements, by midnight Oct. 15, including in the Federal Register, and to keep registration open for 30 days. The department must accept eligible electronic entries, notify those selected and process applications until the visas run out or the fiscal year ends Sept. 30, 2027. The program offers up to 55,000 green cards a year; the administration had not opened registration on time and argued it was too late.

A Singapore-flagged container ship, GFS Pride, sank in the Strait of Hormuz after an unknown projectile hit it, Singapore said; all 21 crew got off safely. Singapore's Maritime and Port Authority said GFS Pride was struck Tuesday, caught fire and sank; no injuries were reported. A second Singapore-flagged container ship, GFS Giselle, took hull damage from a projectile Wednesday but reached a safe anchorage with all 22 crew. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a ship hit naval mines while using what they called an "unauthorised" route. The only other ship reported sunk since the Iran war began in February was the Safeen Prestige in March; the UN's maritime agency counts at least 24 seafarers killed in 106 confirmed incidents.

Consumer prices rose 3.7% over the past year in September, up from 3.4% in August, as gasoline jumped 9.1% in a month. The Bureau of Labor Statistics said its consumer price index rose 0.6% in September after 0.4% in August, with gasoline accounting for over half of the monthly gain. Prices excluding food and energy rose 0.3% for the month and 2.6% over the year (2.4% in August). Energy prices are up 20.4% over 12 months and gasoline 34.2%; food was unchanged for the month. Stocks had their worst day since July: the S&P 500 fell 1.1%, the Nasdaq 1.9% and the Dow 0.1%, AP reported. The October report is due Nov. 10.

The Fed's Beige Book found most of its 12 districts saw little change in consumer spending, with spending driven by high-income households. Two districts reported moderate growth, three modest, four slight and three no significant change since the prior report. Robust manufacturing growth led Dallas, and six other districts reported modest to moderate factory growth. Most districts reported little or no net change in employment. Auto sales were flat to lower in five of six districts that reported, and Boston, Minneapolis and San Francisco noted fewer Canadian tourists. Information was collected on or before Oct. 5; the report feeds into the Fed's Oct. 27-28 rate meeting.

The Justice Department's first national tax fraud surge brought cases against 76 defendants accused of trying to take more than $490 million from the Treasury. DOJ's new Fraud Division, 35 U.S. attorney's offices and IRS Criminal Investigation ran the surge from early September to Oct. 14. Prosecutors brought 23 actions with new charges against 31 defendants, with an alleged intended loss above $350 million, plus about 39 trials, guilty pleas and sentencings involving 45 others (nearly $140 million). The largest case charges four Texas residents with selling a sham-trust tax shelter that allegedly hid more than $1.5 billion of income and cost the IRS over $200 million. Charges are allegations; defendants are presumed innocent.

A Russian drone strike killed six people and injured 13, including a child, in Lutsk in western Ukraine, Ukraine's emergency service said. The State Emergency Service said search and rescue work was finished and one injured person was in critical condition. Drone debris hit a wholesale warehouse, and a nine-story apartment building on Sobornosti Avenue was damaged, officials said. The strike came hours after an overnight Russian attack that cut power to at least 600,000 Ukrainians despite the energy ceasefire Trump announced Sunday.

Bank of America's third-quarter profit fell 17% to $6.9 billion after a $1.2 billion federal penalty, while Morgan Stanley's profit rose to $4.9 billion. Bank of America earned 91 cents a share; excluding the penalty for anti-money-laundering and sanctions failures, it would have been $1.08. Revenue rose 3.2% to $30.1 billion but missed estimates as bond trading revenue fell 17% to $2.55 billion, CNBC reported; net interest income rose 7.9% to $16.6 billion. Morgan Stanley reported net revenue of $20.3 billion, up from $18.2 billion a year earlier, and earnings of $3.03 a share, with $232 billion in net new wealth-management assets.

item.title: Morning Edition, Wednesday, October 14, 2026
item.description:
Russian missiles and drones knocked out power to at least 600,000 Ukrainians overnight and killed three in Kyiv, despite President Trump's claim that both sides had agreed to halt energy strikes. Zelenskyy said the hours-long attack, aimed mainly at Kyiv and Kharkiv, damaged 30 energy facilities, and called it "ostentatious disrespect" toward the United States. Ukraine said it shot down only four of 39 missiles. Russia's Defense Ministry said it struck four power plants in and around Kyiv and two in Kharkiv, among other targets, and Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said attacks also hit state railway facilities in five regions. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv has confirmed the energy truce Trump announced.

The Trump administration's rule for fining migrants up to $998 a day for not leaving the U.S. was made final today, after a Boston judge stayed the earlier version. Homeland Security and the Justice Department finalized the June 2025 interim rule with one change: ICE may accept a late appeal when a documented mail delay was beyond the person's control. Appeals are still due within 15 business days. The rule covers fines for failing to leave after a final removal order (up to $998 a day), missing a voluntary-departure deadline and being caught entering illegally. A federal judge in Massachusetts stayed the interim rule and the fines issued under it, finding ICE likely skipped required public comment; the departments say that stay does not stop the final rule from taking effect immediately. DHS also proposed today to end the rule telling USCIS officers to defer to earlier approvals when deciding H-1B, L-1, O-1 and other work-visa extensions; comments are due Nov. 13.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico keep their White House access for the rest of their lawsuit after a federal judge blocked President Trump's ban late Tuesday. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly in Washington issued a preliminary injunction, replacing the temporary restraining order he granted Sept. 24, and found the outlets likely to win their free-speech and due-process claims. He wrote that Trump likely banned them because he sees their reporting as biased, and noted the national-security reason came after their passes were pulled. The order has no end date but does not require access to the Oval Office or Air Force One. It is not a final ruling on the merits.

ASML, the sole maker of the machines that print advanced AI chips, said its planned supply for 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet customer demand. The Dutch company reported record third-quarter sales of 11.7 billion euros and net income of 5.0 billion euros, up from 9.3 billion and 2.9 billion in the second quarter, with a 57.5% gross margin. It expects fourth-quarter sales of 14.2 billion to 15.2 billion euros and full-year 2026 sales of 44 billion to 45 billion euros. CEO Christophe Fouquet said some customers want to place orders for 2029 and 2030, and ASML is studying ways to add capacity for 2028 beyond the 30% increase it announced earlier.

A federal rule barring Medicaid and CHIP money for puberty blockers, hormones and gender surgery for minors takes effect today in every state. The CMS final rule, published Aug. 13 (91 FR 52406), bars federal Medicaid funding for these procedures for patients under 18 and federal CHIP funding for those under 19. Children already on hormone therapy get up to six months of federal funding to taper; that transition does not cover puberty blockers or surgery. In New Hampshire, families suing in Goe v. HHS were denied a temporary restraining order on Oct. 5; their preliminary-injunction request is still pending, and no court has blocked the rule.

Bank of America was hit with more than $1.21 billion in federal penalties for anti-money-laundering and sanctions violations, Treasury said. Treasury called it the third-largest penalty in its history. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency's $750 million civil penalty, credited toward the total, is the largest the OCC has ever imposed. In its resolution with FinCEN, the bank admitted it willfully violated the Bank Secrecy Act; Treasury said it failed to report on time more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, over $1 billion of it tied to national-security risks such as Chinese money-laundering networks and the southwest border. The bank must hire a third party to find unreported transactions and undergo independent reviews. OFAC separately announced an $11.66 million settlement over 475 apparent sanctions violations. The bank said the penalties mean a $1.2 billion third-quarter charge; it reports earnings Wednesday.

Cornell suspended all parties and social events at its fraternity houses for the rest of the 2026-27 academic year, citing the Jane Doe case. In a letter Tuesday, President Michael Kotlikoff said the suspension covers all Interfraternity Council houses, takes effect immediately and allows a review of whether and how fraternity life can safely continue; any fraternity that holds an in-house party or social event will face an immediate emergency suspension. He apologized for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024. Cornell will also add staff to its Office of Civil Rights and victim-advocate office, and is working with the New York State Police so its investigators, who are independent of the university, can investigate on-campus sexual assault reports while Sally Yates's independent review runs. Attorney General Letitia James's separate criminal investigation continues; no one has been criminally charged, and the men named in the civil lawsuit deny the accusations.

The Supreme Court agreed to decide whether DOGE must turn over records to a watchdog group under the public-records law. In U.S. DOGE Service v. U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (No. 25-1103), the justices granted the Trump administration's appeal in Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington's Freedom of Information Act case. U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled in April 2025 that DOGE likely is an agency covered by FOIA; the administration says DOGE is an advisory body inside the Executive Office of the President and exempt. The Supreme Court in June 2025 ordered the D.C. Circuit to narrow the judge's discovery orders; the D.C. Circuit refused in July to halt the narrowed disclosure. Arguments are expected early in 2027, with a ruling by summer. The court also agreed to hear Blanche v. Ozurumba (No. 25-1343), on whether cooking at a Nigerian separatist group's camp counts as "material support" for terrorism that bars an immigrant from asylum.

Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv overnight with no warning from partners, Zelenskyy said, as a strike on a Kharkiv apartment building killed four. Zelenskyy said Russia attacked overnight with more than 100 drones, loitering munitions and ballistic missiles; five ballistic missiles struck civilian infrastructure in Kyiv, where one person was killed and 11 injured, the UN said. In Kharkiv a residential building was destroyed, four people were killed and 41 injured in one evening. Zelenskyy said Ukraine got no intelligence from partners about the missiles headed to Kyiv; Ukrainian officials said U.S. intelligence sharing continues. He said Ukraine has not struck Russian refineries since President Trump announced an energy ceasefire, while Russia keeps hitting Ukraine's energy sites. On Monday U.S. officials warned they could suspend intelligence sharing.
